docs.t: Found on the Vivobook: a SanDisk stick holding Rudolf OS 1.4.1 (ISO 9660, RUDOLF EFI, RUDOLFDATA) was detected (usb-storage, sda) but not in the File Explorer's drives: devplug's system_disk counted every disk with a RUDOLFDATA or ISO 9660 partition as Rudolf OS's own. Fixed: only the disk Rudolf OS runs from is its own (a partition in use outside /media, or the disk holding the start-up image's file); another Rudolf OS stick's start-up parts are not shown and its RUDOLFDATA is mounted read-only, named "Rudolf OS data (another Rudolf OS, read-only)" (its files are another installation's; accounts there are encrypted). Checked on the Vivobook with the fixed script: sda3 mounted read-only and announced, sda1/sda2 and the internal drive left alone. Test: qt/host/devrudolf59_t.sh 7/7; devunsup_t.sh 18/18.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Asked for after a review of how Rudolf OS stands against malware aimed at its owner (2026-11-14). Below the desktop it is strong: Secure Boot with Rudolf's own keys and a signed kernel image, read-only signed system layers, signed updates and Library packages, the a/b slots and recovery, Chromium's sandbox for websites, sandboxed Library web apps and downloads, the firewall, encrypted home folders. Above it, the review found five gaps; a directed attack would most likely get a program run (a game, an .exe, a Linux app) and go through gap 1. In this order:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Found: rudolfd serves the desktop page, with its per-boot API token and the page's stored data (rudolf-ls), to any program that connects to 127.0.0.1:8080 (serve_index has no check). A Linux app, a Wine program or a Flatpak with network access, all running as uid 1000 like the desktop, can read the token and then drive the API, which runs as root (disks, updates, factory reset, accounts).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Who is connecting: for each connection to 8080 (and every other loopback listener of rudolfd: 8099 and the rest, listed in 15.5), rudolfd finds the socket's process: the peer's port in /proc/net/tcp (and tcp6) gives the socket's inode and uid; the inode is looked for only among the processes of the desktop's cgroup (cgroup.procs: Chromium's, rudolf-webkit's or rudolf-native's processes, and the Chromium of Oracle on Native, Part 12 step 8). Found there: the desktop. Else: not the desktop. Done once per connection (keep-alive keeps the answer).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: What a program that is not the desktop gets: not the page (403, "This page belongs to Rudolf OS's desktop"), no /api/ (403 even with the right token), no rudolf-ls. What stays open to everyone, as now: /lib/ and /pkg/ (shared libraries with CORS for Oracle's sandboxed pages), /dlf/ (downloads, served sandboxed), the Library's web apps (sandboxed, no origin). The other programs must not be in the desktop's cgroup: every program rudolfd or the page starts (Linux apps, Flatpak, Wine, Debian, emulators, the Chromium window for websites on Lite) goes into an apps cgroup of its own, never inheriting the desktop's; checked by a test that starts each kind and reads its cgroup.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Once each account is its own Linux user (15.3): the desktop's uid (rudolf, 1000) is required as well, from the same /proc/net/tcp line: a second check that costs nothing. Tests: host tests of rudolfd: the page and the API from a process in the desktop's cgroup (allowed), from one outside it with the right token (refused), the token never in a refused answer; QEMU: from a Flatpak app, a Wine program and a Debian terminal, curl 127.0.0.1:8080/ and an API call with a token read some other way, both refused; the desktop on each engine unaffected (Standard, Lite, Native, Oracle on Native).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Done (2026-11-14, iso/sys/rudolfd-peer.inc): "/", "/index.html" and every /api/ request are answered only for root and for processes of the desktop's memory group (the peer's socket found in /proc/net/tcp, its inode among the group's processes' descriptors; the last one that answered tried first, RUN/peer-hint). Others get 403 ("only Rudolf OS's desktop may use this"), said in System health under Security (with the Linux user, once a minute at most). A missing or empty desktop group is not enforced (so the desktop is never shut out of its own page), said once in System health and failed by the self-test's new desktop-guard line. Also: Yama in the kernel (SECURITY_YAMA, ptrace_scope 1), so a program cannot read the browser's memory for the token by ptrace either; the self-test's ptrace line checks it. Programs rudolfd starts are already its children, outside the desktop's group; rudolf-native and rudolf-webkit start none of their own. Test: qt/host/peer59_t.sh (17). Still to do from this step: the QEMU check from a Flatpak app, a Wine program and a Debian terminal (with the next beta).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: Found: the built-in apps all run in the desktop's one page (one origin), so a scripting bug in how one app shows a file (a document, an SVG, an HTML or Markdown file, an e-book) would reach every app's data and the token.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: Every place a file's contents become HTML (innerHTML, srcdoc, document.write of file-derived text, inline SVG, data: and blob: documents) is listed by a check (iso/systools/htmlsinks.py, run before each PR like deadcheck) and either escapes the text or shows it in a frame with sandbox and no allow-same-origin (no origin: no storage, no token, no parent), its scripts off unless the app needs them (the PDF viewer's PDF.js, already a sandboxed page). WordLite's and WordPro's .docx, the e-book reader, Markdown and HTML previews, SVG in the picture viewer (as , never inline), File Explorer's previews, Notepad's HTML view, the Help pages from packages.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: The page's own Content-Security-Policy, sent by rudolfd: connect-src limited to rudolfd and the services the desktop names (Open-Meteo, the Library, the update server, the time servers' HTTPS fallback), object-src none, base-uri none, frame-ancestors the shell only; so injected code could not send anything out even if it ran. Inline scripts stay allowed for now (the page is built that way); moving them to hashes is 1.6.0's. Tests: a set of hostile files (scripts in every place each format allows them) opened in each app: nothing runs in the desktop's origin (a canary in the page is never read); the CSP blocks a fetch to an outside address. Done (2026-11-14):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: Found by the hostile-files test (qt/shell2/hostile59_t.js: 19 hostile files, each opened in every app that opens it and by default, 64 openings, plus File Explorer, Open with, Properties, Recent and notifications): the apps already escape names and contents, and Oracle shows HTML and SVG files in frames with sandbox="allow-scripts" only (no origin). One gap: WordPro's clean() was a set of patterns. It kept javascript: links, and a slash in place of a space () or an SVG got script past it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: desktop/sanitize59.js, safeHtml(): the browser's own parser (DOMParser, inert), removes what runs or loads, every on* attribute, srcdoc and formaction, and links and sources other than relative, #, http(s), mailto, tel, blob and data: pictures (not SVG); checked again until it settles, against mutation tricks. WordPro's clean() (opening, pasting) uses it. Test: qt/shell2/sanitize59_t.js (29 ways past a cleaner and 7 kinds of script link, what documents need kept, WordPro itself). iso/systools/htmlsinks.py, run by deadcheck.py: the places that make HTML from data, counted per file against htmlsinks.json (518 in 80 files on 2026-11-14: today's number, the hostile-files test is what checks them); a new one fails the check until it is reviewed and the list updated.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: The page's policy (rudolfd): Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'. connect-src is not limited: Oracle's downloads and the apps' imports fetch from any https address, so a list would stop only plain http. Inline scripts stay allowed (1.6.0). Still to do: the same test on the Vivobook's beta.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: 1.6.0 Part 10, as written there, done in 1.5.9: each account's Linux apps, Wine and Debian run as the account's own user (uid 1001 and up), so one account's programs cannot read another's files, and none is the desktop's user (15.1's second check). 1.6.0 Part 11 (elogind and polkit) stays in 1.6.0. Done, first step (2026-11-14), iso/sys/rudolfd-users.inc:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: Users: each account of the page's list (bd95user, read from the lsync copy after every lsync and at start; not the guest) gets acctUID, uid and gid 1001 and up, with no password, in audio, video, input and group 1000 (the devices' group: cameras, controllers, hidraw, the ADB phone, which mdev gives to group 1000). An account that goes loses its user (its programs stopped); the uids are kept in /persist/etc/rudolf/account-users ("ID UID [moved]", "-ID UID" for a removed one, never given again) and written into /etc (in RAM) at every start.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: Files: the account's folder (/persist/accounts/ID, encrypted with its key) and what is made in it belong to its user, 0700: no other account's user, and not the desktop's, can go in (rudolfd serves the desktop page as root). The move of existing computers: at the first start each account's folder's files owned by the desktop's user become its user's (lchown only, nothing copied), logged ("… belong to its own Linux user now: N moved"); a file that cannot be moved leaves the account to be tried again at the next start, said in the health log (Accounts) and in System health (the new "Accounts' Linux users" line, from GET accounts/users).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: The session: at sign-in with the files on the disk (home_bind) the account's folder is also its user's home (/home/acctUID, a bind), /run/user/UID is its own, its session D-Bus and rudolf-portal start as it, and /run/rudolf/acct-session.env has its environment. Linux apps (rudolf-apps launch) and Flatpak apps (native run) start as the account's user with it; nobody signed in (or an account without its files on the disk, or the guest): as the desktop's user, as before. Sound: the desktop's PulseAudio offers a second socket, /run/rudolf/pulse/native, in a folder for the audio group only (in the list of listeners). Signing out (home_unbind) stops every program of the user (TERM, then KILL), its home and runtime folder go; rudolfd started again in the session keeps them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: 15.1's second check: the page and the API are answered only for the desktop's user (rudolf, 1000) or root, as well as its memory group (rudolfd-peer.inc). Tests: qt/host/users59_t.sh (21, on ext4 with real users in a private namespace: users made, the same again, the move and a file that cannot move, one account's user refused another's files, the session, sign-out stopping every program but another account's, rudolfd started again, an account removed and its uid not given again), peer59_t.sh (20, with 9b: a process of another user in the desktop's group refused), dl140_t.js (System health's line). docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: X authorization instead of -ac: the session makes a new cookie at each start (`rudolf-display --xcookie /run/rudolf/xauth, root's only, FamilyWild) and starts Xvfb and Xorg with -auth (Xvfb also -noreset`, so the list survives the last client); the display is then given by user, X's server-interpreted localuser (the socket's peer, no cookie needed): rudolf-display --xallow root rudolf and the signed-in account's user (from acct-session.env, so an X that starts again for a new resolution keeps it). rudolfd gives it at sign-in (au_xaccess, --xallow acctUID) and takes it back at sign-out (--xdeny). Another account's programs and every other user's are refused. If no cookie can be made, X starts open (-ac) as before and the session log says so (the desktop never fails to start for it). The list of listeners says so (X's two lines).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: Debian and Wine as the account's user: while an account is signed in with its files on the disk, rudolf-debian maps Debian's "rudolf" (1000 inside) onto the account's user (acctUID) instead of the desktop's; its group stays 1000 (the devices' group, which the accounts' users are in). Decided against making a second uid in Debian's passwd: Debian's user, password, sudo and files stay as they are, only who it is outside changes. Its home is the account's folder (so Wine's prefix, ~/.wine, the programs Wine installs and their launchers and icons are the account's; the shell's settings are copied from /etc/skel when the folder has none); its /run/user/1000 is its own tmpfs with the account's session bus and the accounts' sound socket (/run/rudolf/pulse/native) bound in. Debian's own root cannot go into those (they are not its users'), so rudolf-debian places them from outside, as rebind does (open_tree, then move_mount in Debian's mount namespace). The map is made when Debian starts and kept beside its pid (/run/rudolf/debian/init.uid): when the account changes (rebind at sign-in and sign-out, or any command), Debian is stopped and started again for the new user on the next command. With libFuzzer when clang has it, else its own coverage-guided mutation fuzzer under AddressSanitizer and UBSan (this build host has no libFuzzer). Corpus in qt/host/fuzz/corpus (a fixed crash kept as fixed-*). qt/host/fuzz59_t.sh runs it for FUZZ_SECONDS (60; ci_release.sh: 120 before each release). docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-10: plan the first release of Rudolf OS that works with cellular networks, and stage what it needs in 1.5.8 and 1.5.9. It follows the mobile work in docs/plan-1.5.8.md (Parts 6 to 8) and docs/plan-1.5.9.md.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › What "cellular" means in 1.6.0
docs.t: Mobile data, by every common route, on x86 computers: a hotspot or phone on Wi-Fi (works today), a hotspot or phone over USB (1.5.8), a USB cellular stick, and a cellular module built into a laptop or tablet (M.2 WWAN cards: Quectel, Fibocom, Sierra Wireless, Telit). The SIM and the network handled in Rudolf OS: the SIM's PIN (and PUK), the operator's settings (APN) found by themselves, roaming on or off, signal, operator and network type in the taskbar, airplane mode. Living with a data plan: metered connections (1.5.8), data used this month and a limit, Wi-Fi preferred over cellular, and cellular as the fallback when Wi-Fi drops.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › What "cellular" means in 1.6.0
docs.t: Text messages, read and sent through the modem (carrier messages, sign-in codes), in a Messages app. ARM64: the first ARM64 release, for computers that start with UEFI (and QEMU), with the same cellular support. Not in 1.6.0: voice calls and emergency calls (a computer is not a phone, and emergency calling must be tested on each device before it is offered: 1.6.x, with the first phone), phones themselves (1.6.x, docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.3), eSIM provisioning (downloading a carrier's eSIM profile), and 5G standalone features beyond what the modem does by itself. Everything moved past 1.6.0 is gathered in docs/plan-1.6.1.md (2026-11-15).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Leanness
docs.t: Cellular support adds about 6 to 10 MB to the base layer (ModemManager, libqmi, libmbim, libqrtr, the operators' database, the kernel drivers as modules): measured in the release check against a 15 MB budget. (2026-11-15: the owner dropped the size budgets for 1.6.0: the build prints the sizes, systools/ci_release.sh.) ModemManager starts only when a modem is present (mdev starts it on the first modem it sees), so a computer without one runs nothing more. The Messages app is part of the desktop page (no new engine), and keeps messages in the account's folder.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 1. Modems (needs 1.5.9's ModemManager)
docs.t: ModemManager, with QMI, MBIM, QRTR and AT support, in the system layer; its D-Bus API read by rudolfd (mobile/*). FCC unlock: many laptop modules (Lenovo's and Dell's Fibocom and Quectel cards) start with their radio locked until the computer unlocks them. ModemManager's unlock scripts ship but are off; Settings offers "Turn on this laptop's cellular module" for the modules that need it, saying what it does, administrators only. Modules that Linux supports only partly (Intel's XMM7360 in some ThinkPads) are named in Settings with what is known about them, rather than failing silently.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 2. SIM and network (Settings › Mobile network)
docs.t: The SIM: present or not, locked with a PIN (asked once, by an administrator; three tries; the PUK after that, with the warning that a wrong PUK blocks the SIM for good), and the operator. The operator's settings (APN) from mobile-broadband-provider-info, by the SIM's operator code; a custom APN by hand. Roaming: off by default, with what it may cost. Preferred network type (5G, 4G, 3G) where the modem lets it be chosen. Airplane mode in the taskbar's quick settings: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the modem off together (rfkill and ModemManager), and back as they were.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 3. The connection
docs.t: Connect and disconnect from the taskbar; connect automatically (on by default for the SIM's home network). Priority: cable, then Wi-Fi, then cellular; cellular stays connected but unused while Wi-Fi works, and carries the traffic within seconds when Wi-Fi drops (the routes' metrics), with a notification. The firewall applies to the cellular interface as to every other. IPv6 and IPv4 as the operator gives them (many operators are IPv6-only with NAT64/464XLAT: clat where needed).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 4. Data and money
docs.t: Metered by default on cellular (1.5.8's metered connections). Data used this month on each SIM, from the interface counters, kept across restarts; a monthly limit with a warning at 80 % and, if chosen, cellular data off at 100 %; the month's start day set by the person. Updates on cellular: never automatic; offered with the download size ("Download over mobile data: 42 MB").

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 5. Signal and status
docs.t: The taskbar shows signal bars, the network type (5G, LTE, 3G) and the operator, from ModemManager; Settings shows the signal's details (RSRP, RSRQ, SINR) for placing the computer or an antenna. System health: modem events (SIM removed, PIN blocked, no network, the module restarted). The self-test: the modem found, its driver, the SIM, registration, a data connection.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 6. Messages (SMS)
docs.t: A Messages app: conversations, read and send, delivery reports, notifications for new messages (also with the desktop locked: the sender and "new message", not the text, unless the person allows it). Messages kept in the account's folder (.rudolf/messages), and in the encrypted folder when "Encrypt my data" is on. Long messages and Unicode (multi-part SMS); MMS is left out (it needs the operator's MMS gateway and a separate APN).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 7. ARM64 (from 1.5.9's build)
docs.t: The first published ARM64 release: its own update list (beta/arm64/, stable/arm64/), a disc image for UEFI ARM64 computers, and the same parts 1 to 6. Proven in QEMU aarch64 and on one ARM64 computer before it is published.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: In 1.6.0 after all (owner, 2026-11-17: "Skip the test and just add it"): the base side below is in 1.6.0; the usbprint extension is published for the beta by extensions.yml, without a test on a real printer (refined in 1.6.1). Asked for: printing to printers plugged in by USB, as Rudolf OS prints to network printers now (rudolf-print: IPP Everywhere and AirPrint, no CUPS and no drivers). The same print dialog (WordPro, SpreadsheetPro, PresentPro, and the PDF Viewer since 1.5.9) lists them as "USB: name".

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.1 Which USB printers
docs.t: IPP over USB (the USB printer class's protocol 4, 7/1/4; most printers sold since about 2015, and every one with the IPP Everywhere or Mopria logo): the printer speaks IPP over its USB link exactly as over the network. ipp-usb (Debian's, GPL-2) turns it into a local IPP address; rudolf-print then prints to it as to a network printer (PDF, or PWG / Apple raster from pdf.js). Nothing new to write for the job itself. Plain USB printers that read PDF or PostScript (7/1/1 or 7/1/2, the IEEE 1284 device ID listing PDF or POSTSCRIPT in its command set): the job is written to /dev/usb/lpN as it is. Through the kernel's usblp driver.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.1 Which USB printers
docs.t: Others (PCL-only or host-based printers that need a driver): not in 1.5.9. The dialog names the printer and says it needs a driver Rudolf OS does not have; PCL raster from pdf.js (as PWG raster is made now) is a candidate for later.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.2 What changes
docs.t: Kernel: USB_PRINTER (usblp) as a module, checked in kconfig.sh (x86 and ARM64). usblp must not claim an IPP over USB printer's interface 7/1/4 (ipp-usb needs it): the modem service's way (mdev with the interface's class) unbinds it for those. The system layer: ipp-usb and its libraries, with a budget checked in ci_release.sh (about 10 MB expected; the build says the real size, as for ModemManager). Avahi is not added: ipp-usb's address is passed to rudolf-print in /run/rudolf/usb-printers instead of being announced on the network.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.2 What changes
docs.t: /usr/lib/rudolf/usbprint (mdev hotplug, like the modem service): a printer plugged in starts ipp-usb for it (IPP over USB) or records its /dev/usb/lpN and device ID (plain); unplugged, it stops it and forgets it. rudolfd's print/find adds these to the network's printers; print/job sends to /dev/usb/lpN for the plain kind. Settings › Devices lists a USB printer with its kind (IPP over USB, PDF, PostScript, or "needs a driver"). The self-test: a "usb-printer" line (found, its kind, ipp-usb answering).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: Host: the hotplug script with stand-ins (an IPP over USB printer's interfaces, a plain PostScript one, a PCL-only one); rudolfd's print/find listing them; a job to the plain kind written to a stand-in /dev/usb/lp0. rudolf-print against ipp-usb's stand-in (its test IPP server) as for network printers. On real hardware: the HP desktop's user's USB printer (on the HP desktop, or on the Vivobook if it can be borrowed), first read only (its interfaces and device ID: which kind it is), then a test page. Done, first step (2026-11-15), on Part 13's signed system extensions: Kernel: USB_PRINTER (usblp) a module, checked after olddefconfig in kconfig.sh and kconfig-arm64.sh.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: Devices: 90-rudolf.rules runs /usr/lib/rudolf/usbprint for a printer's interface (by ENV{INTERFACE}=="7/1/*", so also when it goes; add, remove and bind) and for usblp's /dev/usb/lpN; mdev's fallback has the same two lines (before its modalias line). udevadm verify passes on the rules.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: /usr/lib/rudolf/usbprint (hotplug, scan): every USB printer there is, written to /run/rudolf/usb-printers (kind, name, address, IEEE 1284 device ID, sysfs name): IPP over USB (an interface 7/1/4: usblp unbound from that printer's interfaces, ipp-usb started in its udev mode, which ends after the last one, and its port read from its state file: ipp://127.0.0.1:PORT/ipp/print; no address without the extension), PDF or PostScript (the device ID's command set: its /dev/usb/lpN), or "needs a driver" (PCL-only, host-based); plugged in and unplugged said in /run/rudolf/usbprint.log; the name from the device's strings or its device ID (short and long field names).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: The first extension, usbprint (iso/ext/usbprint: recipe.json, its start script, its filters' links): ipp-usb (from Ubuntu's /sbin, put in usr/sbin), Poppler's pdftops and pdftocairo (as /usr/lib/rudolf/print/pdftops and pdftocairo), libpoppler and Avahi's client libraries where the base lacks them (mkext.sh leaves out what the base has), ipp-usb's quirks; its start script writes ipp-usb's settings (loopback only, no DNS-SD: Rudolf has no Avahi, the address goes through /run/rudolf/usb-printers instead, ports from 60000, short logs). No budget in ci_release.sh (the base does not carry it); mkext.sh prints its size: about 9.9 MB of files with all its libraries, 2.2 MB to download where the base has libpoppler and Avahi's client (measured here on Ubuntu 24.04, 2026-11-15).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: rudolf-print: find adds the USB printers as "USB: name" (an IPP over USB one at ipp-usb's address, printed to as a network printer; a plain one as usb://lpN; one that cannot print as usb://KIND/SYSNAME); rudolf-print usb (JSON for Settings: kind, ready); info for usb:// (formats; a PostScript one only with the extension's pdftops; one needing a driver has no format, so the print dialog says it needs a driver; an IPP over USB one without the extension says to install it); send to usb://lpN writes the PDF as it is (the pages picked with pdftocairo when the extension is there, else all of them, said) or PostScript from pdftops (with the pages), once per copy.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: rudolfd: print/find as before (with them); print/usb; a printer's address may be usb://... (no "..", quotes or ports). Settings › Devices › Printers plugged in by USB (desktop/usbprint60.js): each one's name (as text) and kind (IPP over USB, reads PDF, reads PostScript, needs a driver), ready or needing the USB printers extension (a System extensions… button), read again with Refresh and when a USB device comes or goes. The self-test: a "usb-printer" line (each one and its kind; fails when an IPP over USB one has no address or ipp-usb does not answer there; skipped with none).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: Tests: qt/host/usbprint60_t.sh 31 (a stand-in sysfs: an IPP over USB printer, a PostScript one, a PCL-only one, a PDF one, a USB stick; ipp-usb's stand-in in front of qt/fakeprinter.py, printed to through its address; the jobs to stand-in /dev/usb/lpN; without the extension; unplugged; rudolfd's address check (fixtures/printuri.c); the rules, mdev's lines, the kernel, the self-test), qt/shell2/usbprint60_t.js 13 (and the print dialog's list), udev60_t.sh 13, pdfprint59_t.js 8; .github/workflows/sysext-check.yml runs both host tests (sysext60_t.sh, usbprint60_t.sh) on pull requests.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: Next: extensions.yml's first run (the owner's) to publish usbprint for the first release with a base ABI; the QEMU check with a USB printer passed through (or QEMU's usb-printer-like device) and ipp-usb itself; on the HP desktop's user's printer (borrowed): first read only (its interfaces and device ID: which kind), then a test page; ARM64's recipe (the file globs are by architecture already; the release ext-ABI16 differs per base).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Why: mdev makes device nodes and runs scripts, but keeps no device database and tells no program about devices. Linux software finds hardware through udev (libudev): ModemManager (1.5.9 needed a workaround: #280), libinput, SDL and Steam's controllers, PipeWire, Waydroid and many Flatpak apps. Each gap became a workaround of its own; 1.6.0's modems and the plans after it (Waydroid, PipeWire, a native or Wayland desktop) lean on udev more. Which udev: systemd-udevd on its own (from Debian's udev package; no systemd as init) or eudev, whichever is smaller and keeps working in the build; measured against a budget in ci_release.sh. The hardware database (hwdb.bin) and the packages' rules (ModemManager's, libinput's, the uaccess/joystick ones) come with it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Rudolf OS's own rules: what /etc/mdev.conf does today (the modem service, devplug's USB and phone events, joystick permissions, drives, cameras, the netplug and thunderbolt scripts) becomes rules in /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/90-rudolf.rules calling the same scripts (their ACTION/MDEV environment mapped to udev's), so the scripts change little. Start-up: rudolf-init starts udevd early, triggers coldplug and waits for it to settle (with a time limit) before the display and the services start. Recovery mode keeps mdev as a fallback: if udevd does not start, mdev does, and System health says so. What it lets go of: the modem service's --test-no-udev and its port reporting (ModemManager finds its ports itself again), devplug's own guesses where udev's tags say what a device is.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Tests: host tests of the rules with udevadm test on stand-in devices; QEMU (start-up time with udev against mdev, self-test lists, the camera, Bluetooth, sound, a controller in Steam plugged in while it runs. Done (2026-11-15), in code; measured and checked on the Vivobook at its first beta (asked for: "Implement the transition to udev as we previously planned, and just plan checks and manual tests to ensure everything still works properly"; no memory budget, as said):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Which udev: systemd-udevd on its own and udevadm, from Ubuntu 24.04's udev package (the base layer's libraries come from it): its helpers (ata_id, cdrom_id, scsi_id, v4l_id, …), its rules, and the hardware database (hwdb.bin, built from its hwdb.d in ci_release.sh), with the libraries the base layer lacks (libsystemd-shared's at its own path). Left out: 71-seat and 73-seat-late (systemd-logind's), 90-vconsole and 99-systemd (systemd's), and 80-net-setup-link (it would rename network interfaces; Rudolf OS's scripts know eth0, wlan0 and the adapters by the kernel's names). The groups its rules name (disk, lp, kmem, dialout, cdrom, tape, render, kvm, sgx) are in /etc/group (ci_release.sh for an existing base layer, mkrootfs.sh for a new one).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Rudolf OS's own rules: /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/90-rudolf.rules, every line of /etc/mdev.conf that set an owner or ran a script: the same owners and modes (as numbers), the same scripts (sound, joyperm, rudolf-debian devices, modem, devplug, thunderbolt, netplug) through /usr/lib/rudolf/udev-run, which gives them mdev's MDEV (the name under /dev, or the interface) beside udev's ACTION, SUBSYSTEM, DEVTYPE, DEVPATH, and starts them in a session of their own so a slow one (mounting a drive, starting ModemManager) never holds up udev. Drivers are loaded by udev's 80-drivers.rules (mdev's modprobe line). The scripts themselves did not change.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Start-up: rudolf-init starts udevd (--daemon --resolve-names=early), checks it answers, announces the devices already there (subsystems, then devices) and waits for them, 15 s at most. If udevd does not start or answer, if udev is not in the build, or with rudolf.udev=0 on the start-up line, mdev does as before. /run/rudolf/devices says which ("udev", or "mdev (why)"); the self-test's new devices line fails on the fallback (skipped when asked for), and when udevd stopped or its database is empty.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: What it let go of: the modem service starts ModemManager with udev as on other Linux (no --test-no-udev, no reports of each port: it finds them through udev itself); with mdev, as in 1.5.9. Debian gets udev's database (/run/udev, read only), so Steam and SDL find controllers as on other Linux; Flatpak binds it into its sandboxes itself. devplug's own guesses were left as they are. Tests: qt/host/udev60_t.sh (13 here: rudolf-init's own lines with stand-ins, its four ways to mdev, udev-run, every mdev.conf script in a rule, the modem service, the self-test's line; with udevadm in CI also udevadm verify and udevadm test on the runner's devices), .github/workflows/udev-check.yml.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: 1. Start-up: /run/rudolf/devices says udev; the self-test's devices line passes; /run/rudolf/udev.log has no errors; start-up to the desktop no slower than 1.5.9's (System health › Last starts: 39 s on 2026111503). 2. Every device the self-test lists: its lines all as on 1.5.9 (sound, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, the camera, the GPU, storage, the listeners); ls -l /dev/input /dev/dri /dev/snd /dev/video* /dev/hidraw*: the owners and modes as under mdev (input root 0640, controllers 1000, dri 0666, snd audio 0660, cameras 1000). 3. Network: the interfaces keep their names (wlan0, eth0, usb0); Wi-Fi connects; the MiFi over USB gets an address (netplug) and shows in Network Settings; unplugged, it goes.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 10. A Linux user for each account (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Moved into 1.5.9 on 2026-11-14 (docs/plan-1.5.9.md Part 15.3), as part of its security work. Why: every Rudolf OS account runs as the same Linux user (rudolf, uid 1000). The desktop keeps the accounts apart, but Linux apps, Wine and Debian run as that one user and can read every account's files (the vault's own note says so). Conventional distributions give each person a Linux user of their own.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 10. A Linux user for each account (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Users: each account gets its own Linux user (uid 1001 and up), made when the account is made, removed when it is removed; its home folder (/home/NAME, still encrypted with the account's key) owned by it and readable by nobody else. The rudolf user stays for the desktop engine itself (the page and rudolfd's helpers). What runs as whom: at sign-in, rudolfd starts the account's session pieces as its user: Flatpak apps, Debian and Wine, the session D-Bus, PulseAudio (or PipeWire later), the portal; signing out stops them. Two accounts signed in one after the other never share a running app.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 10. A Linux user for each account (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Shared things: Downloads and the files the desktop page keeps per account move into each user's home; groups for the devices people use (video, audio, input for controllers, the ADB phone) replace today's chmod to uid 1000. Moving existing computers: the first start of 1.6.0 gives each existing account its user and moves its files (ownership only, no copying), checked and logged; anything that cannot move stays readable to its account and is named in System health. Tests: two accounts on the host and in QEMU: one cannot read the other's files from a Flatpak app, a Debian terminal or Wine; signing out stops the account's apps; the move on an existing data partition.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 11. Sessions and admin prompts for Linux apps: elogind and polkit (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Why: Linux apps ask login1 (systemd-logind) whether to keep the computer awake (a game, a video, a download), who is signed in and which devices the person may use; and they ask polkit for an administrator's password before doing something to the system. Rudolf OS has neither, so these requests fail or are ignored. elogind (logind without systemd): one seat, the signed-in account's session (with Part 10, its own user); apps' inhibitors (sleep, idle, lid) are honoured by Rudolf OS's own power code, which already holds off sleep for video, calls and games; rudolfd reads them through elogind instead of guessing.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 11. Sessions and admin prompts for Linux apps: elogind and polkit (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Where apps ask: looked at before building: Flatpak apps ask the portal (org.freedesktop.portal.Inhibit); Chromium and Electron apps, SDL games, Steam and video players ask org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver or org.freedesktop.PowerManagement.Inhibit on the session bus. Debian's programs and Flatpak apps have no system bus on Rudolf OS, so login1's Inhibit (what elogind would add) is not where Linux apps here ask.

docs.t: rudolf-portal (on each account's session bus, and the desktop user's) answers all three: Inhibit, UnInhibit, the portal's Inhibit and its Request's Close (flags 4 sleep and 8 idle kept; log-out and user-switch are not held), ScreenSaver's GetActive and the rest. Each held request is a file in /run/rudolf/inhibit (rudolf-init: 1733), UID-PID-COOKIE with its flags, the app (a Flatpak app by its ID) and its reason; it goes when the app lets go or leaves the bus, and a portal started again clears its own.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 11. Sessions and admin prompts for Linux apps: elogind and polkit (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: polkit: a Linux app's request for an administrator goes, on Rudolf OS, to Debian's own world (Debian has its own user, password and sudo) or is not possible from a Flatpak sandbox; polkitd on the system itself would have nothing asking it. It would also need its agent to answer as root (polkit-agent-helper-1, setuid) with a password the accounts' Linux users do not have (theirs is the desktop's sign-in), so rudolfd would answer it. So the proposal: leave elogind and polkit out of 1.6.0 (and the 5 MB budget with them), and take them up only if an app or a later part (Waydroid, PipeWire, a Wayland desktop) needs them. Udev's seat rules (71-seat, 73-seat-late) stay out with them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 11. Sessions and admin prompts for Linux apps: elogind and polkit (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Decided (2026-11-15): left out, as asked ("If leaving out elogind and polkit causes no issues or possible conflicts with Rudolf or its cross-distribution compatibility, then let's leave it out"). Checked first: nothing in Rudolf OS asks for either (no program here uses login1 or polkit; the system bus serves only BlueZ, bluealsa and ModemManager, which run without them); a Flatpak app with --system-talk-name=org.freedesktop.login1 gets no answer, as it got none before, and such apps (a few use login1's sleep signal) carry on without it; Debian's programs never had a logind; nothing that ran before changes, and apps made for other distributions keep the standard ways they use here (the portals, the Secret Service, ScreenSaver and PowerManagement). Part 11 is done.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Asked for: a way to add system parts (a driver, firmware, a tool, a printer filter) to one computer without a new release, instead of a conventional package manager. Decided (2026-11-14): not a package manager that changes the base (apt or pacman style: every computer would end up different, updates could fail half-way, the base's signature would no longer cover what runs, and rollback would stop being clean), but signed system extensions: read-only layers over the unchanged base, as systemd's sysext and Fedora's image-based editions do. The base stays one signed image, the same on every computer, with its a/b spare and recovery.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.1 What an extension is
docs.t: An rpk package of a new kind, sysext (iso/sys/rpk.c: the same file format, download, signature check, revocation and rpk install/remove), holding files for the system: usr/bin, usr/lib (programs and libraries), lib/firmware, lib/modules/KVER/extra (kernel modules), usr/lib/udev/rules.d (after Part 9), usr/lib/cups or usr/lib/rudolf/print filters (Part 8), and at most one start script, usr/lib/rudolf/ext.d/NAME.start. builds them). A Library or developer key can never sign one (rpk refuses, as it refuses Library programs today).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.1 What an extension is
docs.t: Tied to the base it was built for: PKGINFO base = ABI (a hash of the base layer's libraries, written into the base as usr/share/rudolf/base-abi by ci_release.sh) and, for kernel modules, kernel = KVER. Kernel modules are built in the same run as the kernel, so they carry its module signature.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.2 How it is put in place
docs.t: At each start, before the desktop (the initramfs, or early in init): every installed, enabled extension that matches this base's ABI (and kernel) is mounted read-only at /run/rudolf/ext/NAME, and the system's /usr, /lib/firmware and /lib/modules/KVER/extra become read-only overlays (overlayfs, lower layers only: the extensions over the base, in a fixed order by name). Nothing is ever written into the base. A file the base already has may not be replaced (checked while assembling): an extension adds, it does not override, so one cannot change what the signed base does. A clash leaves that extension out, named in System health.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.2 How it is put in place
docs.t: Start scripts run as root once the overlays are up (only from system-signed extensions), each with a time limit, their output in the health log. Added while running: a new extension's files are available after a restart, said in the install dialog; a firmware or kernel module extension may offer "Restart now".

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.3 Safety
docs.t: A bad extension cannot stop Rudolf starting: the first start after installing one is a trial (as Native's): if the desktop does not come up, the next start leaves out the extensions installed since the last good start and says so. The start menu's recovery entry and Recovery mode always start without extensions. Updates: before switching slots, rudolf-update fetches each installed extension's build for the new base (the extensions' repository has one per base ABI). One that has no build for it yet is kept but left out after the update, with a notice and System health's line, and comes back when its build appears. An update never fails because of an extension.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.3 Safety
docs.t: Revocation: the signed list's R lines disable an extension at the next refresh, as for Library packages. Only an administrator installs or removes one (the administrator's password), and the self-test lists the extensions in use and fails on a clash or a mismatch.

docs.t: Found on the Vivobook (2026-11-14): signing in to the Claude app for Linux with an e-mail address showed a notice that GNOME Keyring is not set up. Linux apps (the Claude app, VS Code, Chromium-based and Electron apps, mail and chat apps) keep their sign-ins and tokens through the Secret Service (org.freedesktop.secrets, libsecret). Rudolf OS has none, so they warn, keep the secret in a plain file (Electron's basic text store) or forget it and ask again after every restart.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: The service: gnome-keyring-daemon's secrets component only (no SSH or GPG agent, no GUI of its own), in Debian's container and for Flatpak apps (the portal's Secret interface), started with the account's session pieces (1.5.9's Part 15.3: each account its own Linux user, so each account its own keyring, in its own encrypted home). Unlocked by the sign-in: the keyring's password is the account's own; the sign-in (and the lock screen) hand it to the daemon (as pam_gnome_keyring does) so no second password is asked; changing the account's password changes the keyring's; signing out locks it. An account without a password gets a keyring kept with the account's encryption key instead of a password.

docs.t: The service: /usr/lib/rudolf/keyring, started by rudolfd at sign-in (au_session_start, after the session bus and the portal) as the account's Linux user with its session's environment: gnome-keyring-daemon `--foreground --components=secrets` (no SSH or GPG agent, no window), on the account's session bus, which Debian's programs (its /run/user/1000/bus) and Flatpak apps with --talk-name=org.freedesktop.secrets reach. Signing out stops it with the account's other programs. Its log: /run/rudolf/keyring-UID.log; its socket ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/keyring/) is in the list of listeners.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Unlocked by the sign-in, without the password: decided instead of handing the password to the daemon. The keyring is the account's "login" keyring in its own folder (~/.local/share/keyrings), made the first time as a keyring with no password of its own (gnome-keyring's text format) and the default. The folder is encrypted with the account's key, is only its user's (0700, the files 0600), and is there only while the account is signed in: so no second password is asked, a password change needs nothing, sign-out shuts it away, and removing the account removes it. A keyring already there (one made in Debian with a password, say) is never changed.

The desktop's own processes keep "Rudolf". Budget: gnome-keyring-daemon and the libraries the base layer lacks, 3 MB, checked in ci_release.sh (the release workflow installs gnome-keyring on the build machine).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: The Secret portal for Flatpak apps (rudolf-portal, org.freedesktop.portal.Secret version 1): libsecret inside a Flatpak sandbox keeps the app's secrets in a file of its own (~/.var/app/ID/data/keyrings), encrypted with a secret the portal gives it through RetrieveSecret(fd). That secret is the app's own (64 random bytes), made once and kept in the account's folder (~/.local/share/rudolf/app-secrets/ID, 0700/0600): so it is as safe as the keyring, the same each time, another app's different. A program outside a sandbox is refused (it uses the Secret Service).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: rudolf-portal is gcr's prompter (org.gnome.keyring.SystemPrompter on the account's session bus, which gnome-keyring-daemon asks; gcr-prompter, a GNOME window, is not in Rudolf OS): gcr's protocol as gcr-system-prompter.c speaks it (org.gnome.keyring.internal.Prompter's BeginPrompting, PerformPrompt and StopPrompting; the daemon's org.gnome.keyring.internal.Prompter.Callback PromptReady and PromptDone; one prompt at a time, the others waiting; the properties sent back as gcr sends them, a new password's strength among them, so the daemon asks "Store passwords unencrypted?" only for an empty one), and its secret exchange "[sx-aes-1]" as gcr-secret-exchange.c does it (Diffie-Hellman in IKE's 1536-bit group, HKDF-SHA256 to a 16-byte key, AES-128-CBC with PKCS#7 padding, its key-file messages), with OpenSSL's libcrypto, which the base layer already has (no new library; the portal is built with -lcrypto in mkrootfs.sh, ci_release.sh and the ARM64 check). Weak public keys (1, p-1, p) are refused.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: The question goes to the desktop as the portal's others do (a request in /run/rudolf/portal/req, kind "keyring": the daemon's title, message, description and warning, a new password or not, its choice, its buttons' words), drawn in keyring60.js in Settings' prompt style (the administrator's prompt: 🔑, who asked, the daemon's words as text, the password fields that hide what is typed, a new one asked twice and a mismatch said, the choice as a tick box), in front of the app on the screen (promptFront). The answer (yes with the password, or no) goes back through portal/answer; rudolfd now writes answers 0600 and owned by the user whose portal asked (they were 0644). The portal reads it, wipes it and hands the password to the daemon encrypted. A question the daemon withdraws (the app went away) is removed, and the desktop closes it.

A local index. rudolfd (a new ai/index part of the engine's API) keeps a searchable index on the data partition, built and brought up to date when the computer is idle and on mains power (never during a game, a call or on battery below 50 %), a few minutes at a time: Rudolf OS itself: the source archive each release already has (rudolf-os-VERSION-source.tar.xz, downloaded once per version with the update, checked against its .sha256) and its docs (README, CHANGELOG, the plans, INSTALL.TXT); shared by all accounts.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 18. Blitzen knows the system: its source, its logs, your activity, and the web through Oracle (added on 2026-11-18)

Kept in that account's part of the data partition; "See what Blitzen knows" lists it; "Forget" by item, by day or all. Text in chunks of about 300 words with where each came from (a file and line, a log and time); found by words (SQLite's FTS5 with BM25) and, when the model's own embeddings are available, by meaning too. About 20-60 MB in all.

Before each answer Blitzen asks the index for what fits the question and the app it is asked from, and puts the best few pieces (within its context, about 2,000 words) into the prompt; the answer names them ("from rudolf-native.c, line 1661"; "the health log, 05:09 today"), each a link that opens the file or the log there. Off for a question with "Without looking it up". The context packs (blitzpacks26.js) stay as they are.

docs.t: 4. The web through Oracle, when asked. A "Search the web" switch on the question (off by default: Blitzen is promised to work offline). On: Blitzen writes a search from the question alone (never the logs, the activity, the files or the memory), runs it through Oracle's engine (over Tor when Oracle's "Use Tor" is on), reads the first few results' pages (at most 5, text only, as Oracle's reader view takes them), and answers from them with numbered sources, links that open in Oracle. What was read is kept for that chat only. The search engine: Oracle's own choice.

A larger model offered on computers with 8 GB or more. As built (2026-11-18): iso/sys/rudolf-know.c (run by rudolfd as root; reads the web as nobody) and rudolfd's ai/know/... (iso/sys/rudolfd-know.inc: status, search, show, learn, activity, list, forget, web); the page's side is desktop/blitzknow60.js (blitzen26.js's ask calls it). Differences from the plan above:

docs.t: The index is plain files in /persist/os/know (chunks of about 300 words with their file and line, or log and line) searched by words with BM25 (with the parts of names split at _ and English endings taken off), not SQLite: no new library in the base layer. Fetched once per release, idle 10 minutes (so never during a game), on mains power or a battery at 50 % or more, not on a metered connection, at the idle priority. A computer started from the disc (no slot) has the logs only.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 18. Blitzen knows the system: its source, its logs, your activity, and the web through Oracle (added on 2026-11-18)
docs.t: The logs are read again before a search when older than a minute (what failed a moment ago is in them), with rudolfd's ai/facts rules (a line with a password, token or key left out; long key-like runs hidden). The activity is kept only while the account's switch is on (rudolfd checks it; the account is the one signed in, never one the page names), at most 2 MB an account (the oldest dropped). Turning it off asks whether to forget what was kept. The memory notes are kept in the page's storage per account (never sent to rudolfd or anywhere but the model).

The pieces, in the base layer (about 4 MB). docs.t: Never in Oracle's Tor windows (the owner, 2026-11-19: "Would using Tor possibly cause issues with either CACs/smart-cards or hardware keys?", then "Yes please" to keeping the card out of them). A card names its holder (a CAC: name and DoD ID number), so it undoes what Tor is for, and the DoD's sites refuse Tor's exits anyway. The Tor Chromium (session tor_chrome, --class=RudolfTor) keeps its own certificate database with no card module (its own HOME for NSS, made fresh for each Tor session; p11-kit's proxy never loaded), so a site reached through Tor that asks for a certificate gets none, and the card is never asked for its PIN there. Settings › Smart cards says so ("Not used in Tor windows"). Hardware keys at Rudolf OS's own sign-in (Part 17 of plan-1.6.1) never use the network, so Tor does not touch them.

docs.t: The DoD's certificates are the computer's, not each account's: Oracle's Chromium has one certificate database for every account (the desktop's Linux user's), so an administrator installs or removes them, for everyone. The roots are pinned by SHA-1 thumbprint, as DISA publishes them in its STIGs (DoD Root CA 3 D73CA911…, 4 B8269F25…, 5 4ECB5CC3…, 6 D37ECF61…; Windows 11 WN11-PK-000005, Windows Server 2019 V-205648), not SHA-256: DISA publishes no SHA-256 list. The bundle's address is read from the DoD PKI's document library page (a link ending certificates_pkcs7…dod.zip), only from dl.dod.cyber.mil, dl.cyber.mil or public.cyber.mil; the desktop checks every certificate's signature, link by link, up to a pinned root (RSA and ECDSA), and leaves out the rest.

docs.t: Written for plan-1.6.1 as Part 18 and moved here the same day (the owner: "Put it in 1.6.0 instead"). The owner (2026-11-19): "Keep it as option 1 for native and lite, and option 2 for standard." An account's files are encrypted with its password key; Oracle's website data (cookies that keep it signed in to sites, site storage, cache, saved site passwords) is kept per account since 1.6.0 Part 21 but lies on RUDOLFDATA unencrypted. Anyone who reads the drive (pulled, or started from another stick) could use those sessions without the Rudolf OS password; two-step sign-in does not change that. Today Chromium runs with --password-store=basic (session, rudolfd's torwin and shell Chromium, rudolf-shellfix): its cookie and password "encryption" uses a key built into Chromium, the same everywhere. RUDOLFDATA has been made with -O encrypt since 1.5.0 (install.sh), so ext4's per-folder encryption (fscrypt) needs no reformat.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 22. Oracle's website data encrypted (added on 2026-11-19)
docs.t: 1. Native: each account's Oracle profile in an encrypted folder (fscrypt). Oracle's Chromium on Native starts after sign-in and closes at sign-out (1.6.0 Part 21's "logout"). Its profile (--user-data-dir) moves to a folder of the account's own on RUDOLFDATA with an fscrypt v2 policy; its key, derived from the account's password key (HKDF, its own label, never the key itself), is added to the kernel's keyring by rudolfd at sign-in (desktop/login, unlock) and removed at sign-out (FS_IOC_REMOVE_ENCRYPTION_KEY), after Chromium has closed. The folder is then names and contents unreadable. Guest stays in memory (its partition is never written). Everything is covered: cookies, site storage, cache, saved site passwords. The website data from before is moved in once (the move said; not kept unencrypted). A drive whose file system lacks encrypt (made before 1.5.0) keeps today's way and Settings says why.

The shell in 1.6.0 (Part 12 above), the apps in 2.0 (docs/plan-2.0.md). The reasoning below is kept as it was written.) Before the first phone (1.6.x), decide whether Rudolf OS's shell becomes native (drawn by its own program, not by a web engine). docs.t: Then: if it saves enough on a 2 to 4 GB device, the phone's shell starts native, and the desktop can follow as Rudolf OS 2.0 (every app moved over, the browser build and the phone web app kept or retired). If not, the web desktop stays and the effort goes into slimming it further. For scale (2026-11-12): Standard at idle about 1.0 to 1.2 GB; light native Linux desktops (Xfce, LXQt) typically 300 to 500 MB for the whole system. The desktop is about 4.9 MB of code in 97 files: a native desktop rewrites all of it, so it is a release of its own, never part of another.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › The phone, split in two (owner, 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Decided on 2026-11-15, after asking whether the first real phone would be easier in 2.0 than in 1.6: "Make the sensible split." 2.0 brings the two things a phone people carry needs most, Wayland (touch gestures, rotation, scaling, the on-screen keyboard, power-saving drawing) and native apps (a fraction of the memory, so a day on the battery), but not the hardest part: making Rudolf OS run on one particular phone. So the phone comes in two stages:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › The phone, split in two (owner, 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Stage 1, here in 1.6.1: the hardware. Rudolf OS boots on one ARM64 phone and its hardware works: the modem's data, texts and voice calls, emergency calls checked, the call's sound, sleep with the modem waking it, charging and the battery. It runs today's native desktop (X11) as it is: proving the hardware, not the phone's interface (Parts 2, 4, 6 and 7 below). Stage 2, in 2.0: the phone build. The phone's own interface on Wayland, the three swipe panels, and native apps laid out for touch, on the hardware stage 1 proved (docs/plan-2.0.md, "The phone build"). Nothing on a phone is flashed or unlocked without the owner's decision.

docs.t: The choice: no CUPS. 1.6.0's driverless printing (rudolf-print: IPP Everywhere, AirPrint, ipp-usb's IPP over USB, plain USB printers reading PDF or PostScript) stays; what 1.6.1 adds is a print queue of Rudolf OS's own in front of it, rudolf-printq (iso/sys/rudolf-printq.c), so that the Linux apps print too and Settings shows the queue:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 9. USB printers and the first ARM64 release (moved from 1.6.0 on 2026-11-16) › 9.1 Status: USB printers and the print queue (2026-11-21, branch usb-printers-161; print-check.yml)
docs.t: One socket, no network listener: /run/cups/cups.sock, where CUPS's own clients look. It speaks the part of IPP over HTTP that CUPS's client library uses (the printers: CUPS-Get-Printers, CUPS-Get-Default, Get-Printer-Attributes; jobs: Print-Job, Create-Job with Send-Document, Validate-Job; the queue: Get-Jobs, Get-Job-Attributes; cancelling: Cancel-Job, Cancel-Jobs, Cancel-My-Jobs, Purge-Jobs as one's own), so lp, lpstat, cancel, GTK's and Qt's print dialogs and LibreOffice print as on any Linux. Debian's /run/cups is this folder (rudolf-debian's print_bind), and Flatpak's cups socket finds it at /var/run/cups (rudolf-init makes /var/run). PDF only (what CUPS's clients send when a printer's formats are PDF; PostScript and others are refused, saying so).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 9. USB printers and the first ARM64 release (moved from 1.6.0 on 2026-11-16) › 9.1 Status: USB printers and the print queue (2026-11-21, branch usb-printers-161; print-check.yml)
docs.t: Each job its sender's: the kernel says who is at the other end (SO_PEERCRED; a Debian program's user is the account's own Linux user, as Debian's user namespace maps it). Only that user cancels a job; the queue lists other users' jobs as "Another account's document", without their names, users or messages. Root (rudolfd) says for whom it asks (X-Rudolf-As: the signed-in account's Linux user, au_app_user, or rudolf) and is held to that user's jobs the same way; anyone else saying so is ignored. (For Part 11's drop: once rudolfd runs as uid 1000 it is no longer root to the queue, so its jobs would be the desktop user's; the account must then come another way, such as a helper of rudolf-rootd's that hands the queue rudolfd's word, never by trusting uid 1000, which the browser has too.)

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 9. USB printers and the first ARM64 release (moved from 1.6.0 on 2026-11-16) › 9.2 Status: Find printers with the firewall on (2026-11-21, branch printer-mdns; mdns-check.yml)
docs.t: The owner, 2026-11-21: "Yes" to fixing network printer discovery for 1.6.1. The bug (the owner's Vivobook, 1.6.0, read-only evidence: find listed no printer in about 2 s and the firewall's blocked counter rose during it): find asked its multicast DNS question from an ephemeral port; printers answer by multicast to 224.0.0.251:5353, which the firewall did not let in (and the socket had not joined the group), or by unicast from their own address, which conntrack does not see as a reply to a question sent to the group (ct state new): every answer was dropped. The tests had pointed RP_MDNS at a stand-in by unicast, which never meets the firewall.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 9. USB printers and the first ARM64 release (moved from 1.6.0 on 2026-11-16) › 9.2 Status: Find printers with the firewall on (2026-11-21, branch printer-mdns; mdns-check.yml)
docs.t: rudolf-print find is now a full querier (RFC 6762): bound to port 5353 (SO_REUSEADDR: rudolfd's find and the print queue's may run at once; Rudolf OS has no Avahi), joined to 224.0.0.251 on each interface that is up (IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP; not loopback, point-to-point or a cellular modem's, the firewall's own /run/rudolf/firewall-cellular), the question sent out of each of them, so printers answer by multicast. It reads only responses (QR set) from source port 5353 (RFC 6762 6), arriving on a joined interface (IP_PKTINFO), not from this computer's own addresses (a program here cannot pose as a printer to other users' finds), and only the groups it joined (IP_MULTICAST_ALL off, its own questions not looped back). The group is left and the port closed when find ends (about 4 s). RP_MDNS unchanged for the tests. parse_mdns's limits stay (64 services, 64 addresses, 20 compression hops, every length checked); a fuzz test now covers it (iso/qt/host/fuzz/mdns_fuzz.c: none existed). The QU bit is not set: a unicast answer to port 5353 needs the firewall's second rule below, a multicast one does not, so multicast is asked for.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 9. USB printers and the first ARM64 release (moved from 1.6.0 on 2026-11-16) › 9.2 Status: Find printers with the firewall on (2026-11-21, branch printer-mdns; mdns-check.yml)
docs.t: The firewall: a chain of its own, mdns, after remote and hotspot and before the drop: iifname @cellular return (never on a cellular interface, as the remote chain), then `ip daddr 224.0.0.251 udp sport 5353 udp dport 5353 accept (an mDNS answer to the group: 224.0.0.x is link-local, never forwarded by a router) and ip saddr { private and link-local IPv4 } ip ttl 255 udp sport 5353 udp dport 5353 accept` (a printer that answers by unicast to the question's source, port 5353 now; TTL 255 means no router lowered it, so the sender is on this link: RFC 6762 11's check). No udp sport 5353 rule to other ports: an answer to an ephemeral port is not needed any more, and the host test checks that a packet from 5353 to another port is dropped. No IPv6 rule: find asks over IPv4 only (the A records are what it prints to), so ff02::fb is not opened. Always on, not only while find runs: find runs both as root (rudolfd) and as the print queue's unprivileged "print" user, which cannot change nftables; opening the port only during find would need a new root helper the queue's user may call,

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5)
docs.t: The aim: every operation that needs root moves into a small helper program that rudolfd runs with checked arguments; rudolfd drops to the rudolf user (uid 1000) once it has started and opened what it must. The areas (one PR each, in this order, each keeping the API byte for byte): drives (mount, unmount, eject, format, the encrypted home's unlock), updates (rudolf-update's slots, roll back, tostable: much is already a separate program), accounts (the per-account Linux users of 1.6.0 Part 10: useradd, chown, the keyring), power (restart, shut down, sleep, brightness), network (Wi-Fi, the firewall, the hostname), packages (rpk, Flatpak's system parts), and whatever a sweep for root-only calls finds (/sys writes, /dev access, mount, kill of others' processes).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5)
docs.t: Each helper: one job, its arguments validated again inside it (never trusting rudolfd), callable only by rudolfd (the rudolf user, checked by SO_PEERCRED on a root-owned socket, or a setuid helper owned root:rudolf mode 4750, whichever the area suits), logged, and small enough to read in one sitting. Never: a weaker check than today's (the token, the peer check of 1.5.9, administrator prompts), or a change the page or the native desktop can see.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5) › 11.2 The design (2026-11-17)
docs.t: One broker, rudolf-rootd, which starts rudolfd (iso/sys/rudolf-rootd.c). rudolf-init runs `rudolf-rootd /usr/bin/rudolfd: it makes a socket pair, starts rudolfd with one end (RUDOLF_ROOTD_FD`; rudolfd makes it close-on-exec at once) and keeps the other. It listens on nothing: no socket in the file system, no port. For a request rudolfd makes a socket pair of its own and passes one end over that first one; rudolf-rootd then checks who made it (SO_PEERCRED: root, or rudolf (1000) once rudolfd drops to it; and that process's /proc/PID/exe is the program it started), reads one message on it (RRQ1, the helper's name, its arguments, each ending in a zero byte, and three descriptors: the helper's standard input, output and error; iso/sys/rudolf-root.h) and runs /usr/lib/rudolf/root/NAME with exactly those arguments (execve, never a shell), with an empty environment (only PATH), its working folder /, umask 022, every other descriptor closed and every signal back to its default; it answers with four bytes, the exit status (254 refused, 253 not started). An unknown name, a malformed message, a request from another user or another program is refused and said in the health log (Security).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5) › 11.2 The design (2026-11-17)
docs.t: Why not the socket in the file system checked by SO_PEERCRED and /proc/PID/exe (the first idea): once rudolfd runs as uid 1000, any program of that user can start its own copy of /usr/bin/rudolfd with LD_PRELOAD, or trace one (not set-user-ID, so the user's own), and that copy's /proc/PID/exe is rudolfd too: the check would let it in. The descriptor handed over at rudolfd's start cannot be had that way: rudolfd is not traceable by the user (it becomes non-dumpable when it drops; PR_SET_DUMPABLE 0 is set explicitly in the drop's step), and nothing it starts inherits the descriptor. The exe check is kept as a second line (a descriptor leaked by mistake still lets nothing else in).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5) › 11.2 The design (2026-11-17)
docs.t: Why not set-user-ID helpers (root:rudolf 4750): every process of the group could run them (the desktop's browser is uid 1000 too), with whatever environment, descriptors, limits and working folder it chooses (the classic set-user-ID mistakes), and rudolfd could not set no_new_privs (it stops set-user-ID). One broker gives every area the same check in one place, a clean start for each helper, and leaves no_new_privs possible. No area needs set-user-ID, so every area uses the broker. The cost: one more small root process, which parses only fixed messages from rudolfd.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5) › 11.2 The design (2026-11-17)
docs.t: Each helper is a program of its own (root:root 0700 in a folder of root's, 0755; never set-user-ID), one area, small enough to read in one sitting. It checks every argument again itself, whatever rudolfd checked: device names letters and digits only and ones the kernel has (/sys/class/block, /sys/block for whole disks); paths made canonical (realpath: no "..", every link followed) and kept inside their allowed root (a link out of it is refused), files plain (not a link) and owned by the desktop's user or the signed-in account's user (another account's file, or a hard link to one, is refused); account names from the account list (/persist/etc/rudolf/account-users), never from rudolfd's word alone; keys and passwords on standard input, never as arguments (anyone can read a process's arguments); the scripts it hands work to are run with argument lists, never a command line for a shell. A refusal is said in the health log (Security), as is anything that erases or rewrites a disk; routine actions (mount, unmount) are not, to keep the log readable. rr_health writes the health log's format ({"t","k","m"}).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5) › 11.2 The design (2026-11-17)
docs.t: rudolfd's side (iso/sys/rudolfd-root.inc): root_call (the helper's status, as run() gave a command's), root_run, root_out (its output, as run_out(), read while it runs), root_job (as start_job: job.name, job.log, job.status). Started without rudolf-rootd (an older rudolf-init, or the QEMU tests that start rudolfd again by hand) and running as root, rudolfd runs the helper itself in the same clean way; so every step works whether or not the drop is on, and the API is the same byte for byte either way (the host test compares them).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5) › 11.2 The design (2026-11-17)
docs.t: The drop (the last step, behind a switch until every area has moved, default off): rudolfd starts as root (from rudolf-rootd), does what must be done before (opens 127.0.0.1:8080, which needs no root as a port above 1023; reads the start-up facts; makes RUN/d, its own folder, rudolf's 0700, for the files it writes; the health log made rudolf's 0600: the helpers still append to it as root), then setgroups to rudolf's own groups (audio and video for the screenshot of /dev/fb0), setresgid and setresuid to 1000, checks it cannot go back (setuid(0) fails), and sets PR_SET_DUMPABLE 0. No capabilities are kept (none is needed: binding 8080 does not need one, reading /proc/net/tcp and the desktop's own processes' descriptors for the peer check of 15.1 is allowed to the same user). The switch: a build flag (RUDOLFD_DROP) and, for testing, rudolf.rudolfd_drop=1 on the start-up options; the default turns on only when every area of 11.1 has moved and the QEMU checks pass with it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 11. rudolfd's root work split into helpers (added on 2026-11-16; from docs/plan-1.5.9.md 15.5) › 11.2 The design (2026-11-17)
docs.t: no_new_privs: rudolfd sets it after the drop if nothing it starts still needs set-user-ID. Today two would: su (the clipboard: unneeded once rudolfd is the desktop's user) and Chromium's chrome_sandbox (4755) for the windows rudolfd starts (websites on Lite, Tor windows); with no_new_privs Chromium cannot use it and needs its namespace sandbox, which needs unprivileged user namespaces. So: no_new_privs is set on rudolfd itself only if the QEMU checks show Chromium's windows still start with it; otherwise those windows are started through a helper and no_new_privs is set in every other child rudolfd starts (prctl in the child before exec). rudolf-rootd's helpers are unaffected either way (they are rudolf-rootd's children, not rudolfd's).

docs.t: What Standard does, checked in its page and in Chromium (xdrop161_std.js): a file dropped anywhere on the desktop goes into the Desktop folder, also over a folder's icon or the Trash (their own drop handlers take only the page's own drags; the drop then reaches the desktop's: shell25.js), named as the page names files (upper case, NAME - COPY.EXT on a clash), kept as text or as a data: URL by its type, over 64 MB refused ("Too large"); dropped text (no file) is refused; the taskbar takes no drop and raises no window.
