docs.t: Moved to 1.6.0 (the owner, 2026-11-19: "All four into 1.6.0"; one beta when all are built). Built there; this text stays the plan. The owner, 2026-11-19: "The version made on the stick and the repository that updates are checked for should come from whatever the set update address is written as by the computer's admin-level user. The system should be able to check that the set update repository is set-up/working correctly and that it is able to match the user's key to it. The intent is for people to be able to roll out their own updates but only to computers that are running the key specific to their own version/build of Rudolf OS. USB sticks pull directly from whatever the set update address is, and still checks to ensure it is set up properly before it attempts to make a copy of that repository's version of Rudolf OS. This is intended for people to be able to download and use each-other's builds." Decided the same day: sticks offer both (the address first, "This Rudolf OS" kept for use without internet); another key's build is allowed on a stick after a warning; Get beta versions keeps the repository that is

An update installs only when its release list is signed by a key the running system trusts (the build's rpk-keys, plus Developer mode's extra-keys): that part of the intent is already true and stays as it is. But Get beta versions overwrites the box with the build's own …/beta (and …/stable when turned off); nothing says whether an address works before an update fails; and Make a USB stick never downloads: it copies the running system (or an image already in Downloads), its boot files from the running release's own boot.iso.

Today the start-up side already holds: the boot menu's Recovery mode (recovery.efi, its own small initramfs with the official key alone) starts only a system/r whose list the official key signed, whatever the update address or Developer mode. What is missing:

docs.t: Kept newest. rudolf-update fetches the official recovery system once (recovery-fetch) and never again. Each update check (whatever the address) also reads the official stable list (OFFICIAL_URL, the official key alone); when its serial is newer than system/r's, the new one is downloaded beside it (r.new, the layers system/r already has linked), checked, and swapped in at once, with recovery.efi from that release's boot.iso; the old one stays until the new one is complete. Not while in recovery mode, and never from the update address, a beta, or Developer mode's key.

docs.t: On every stick. Today a stick's rescue slot is a copy of the stick's own system (os_rescue). Instead, whatever the stick's system (this Rudolf OS, an image, the update address, another person's build): its system/r is the official newest stable (this computer's own when it is that, else downloaded and checked as above) and its recovery.efi is the official one. A stick is not made without it ("Connect to the internet: a stick always gets the official recovery system").

Its boot files may bring their own rudolf.efi, but recovery.efi is always the official one (bootfiles.sh and install.sh keep the official file; the start-up file check of 1.6.0 Part 15 reports any other); and its updates never write system/r. Settings › Update and recovery says which official release Recovery mode starts, and when it was last renewed. What does not change. Updates never install across keys. "Return to official" keeps using the official address. "New boot files" (Secure Boot) keeps its own image choice, with the official recovery.efi beside it. Built in 1.6.0 (2026-11-19), and where it differs from the text above.

docs.t: How it is today. User Settings › Sign-in options › "Add a security key or passkey…" (settings25.js, WebAuthn): the desktop page checks the key's signature after the password. It guards the sign-in screen only: the account's file key (fk) is opened by the password alone (PBKDF2, ks), so a copy of the disk needs only the password; the check is the page's, not the system's; Native and Lite refuse such an account (desktop/accounts key); there is one key and no backup; no authenticator codes. 1. Hardware security keys, read by the system (all three engines).

Not the browser's WebAuthn: WebKit and the native shell have none that can do item 2.

docs.t: Adding one (User Settings › Sign-in options › Security keys › Add): password first, then touch the key (and its PIN, if it has one: asked on screen, never kept). Each account may have up to 5, with names ("Blue YubiKey"); the screen asks for a second one as a spare ("If you lose your only key, only a recovery code or an administrator can let you in"). Signing in: password, then "Touch your security key" (any of the account's). A key with a PIN asks for it (the key counts wrong PINs itself and locks after 8).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 17. Two-step sign-in, done properly (added on 2026-11-19)
docs.t: 2. The key unlocks the files, not only the screen. For an account with a security key, its file key is no longer wrapped by the password alone: each security key gets its own copy of fk, wrapped with HKDF-SHA-256(password key ‖ the key's hmac-secret output for this account's salt) (FIDO2 hmac-secret: the key computes it inside, from a secret that never leaves it). The password-only copy is deleted (and overwritten) when the first key is added. So a copy of the disk, with the password, opens nothing without one of the keys. The same goes for accounts' copies. Keys that cannot do hmac-secret (very old U2F-only ones) are refused when added, with that reason.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 17. Two-step sign-in, done properly (added on 2026-11-19)
docs.t: A recovery code (24 letters and digits in 6 groups, shown once, "write it down or print it") is one more copy of fk, wrapped with the code (PBKDF2, 600 000 rounds). It signs in without a key once, then asks to add a key or make a new code. Administrators' copies (a.ak, 1.5.0) stay, on by default: an administrator can still open the account's files and reset its password (the person's keys are then removed: they add them again). The person can turn them off (User Settings › Sign-in options: "Administrators can open my files", as now), after a warning: "If you lose your keys and your recovery code, nobody can open your files."

docs.t: 3. Authenticator-app codes (TOTP). Six-digit codes every 30 seconds from an app (Google or Microsoft Authenticator, Aegis, 2FAS, …). Adding: a QR code and the text secret, then a code to confirm. Signing in: password, then the code (one step either side of now accepted; a code used once is not taken again). Codes guard the sign-in only: the secret is kept wrapped by the account's password key, so it cannot add anything to the encryption, and Settings says so ("A security key also protects your files if the disk is copied; a code does not."). An account may have a security key, codes, or both (either one is enough at sign-in).

Every sign-in goes through rudolfd (desktop/login, as Native's does now): the password, then the second step, then the file key opened and handed to the signed-in page (as Native's). The page no longer opens fk itself for such an account. rudolfd counts failures: after 5 wrong passwords or codes for an account, a wait (30 s, doubling to 15 min), recorded in System health; a security key needs no count (it is touched). The lock screen asks again (password and the second step; administrators may set "the key alone unlocks the lock screen while signed in").

The Guest account cannot have one and is turned off while "every account" is set. 6. The old page-checked keys. Accounts with one keep signing in on Standard as now; Settings shows "Set up again to protect your files and use Native and Lite" until the key is added again under item 1 (then the old one is removed).

Built in 1.6.0 (2026-11-19): items 3, 4 (in part) and 5; items 1, 2 and 6 later (the owner: "Codes now, keys after": security keys that unlock the files come in their own beta, tested first with a simulated key in QEMU and then the owner's real key, because a mistake there would lock people out of their own files).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 19. Gaming on stronger computers (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: Asked on 2026-11-20 how Rudolf OS games on high-end hardware. Found then: AMD and Intel graphics use Mesa (close to Windows through Steam and Proton); NVIDIA cards have only NVK (iso/systools/addnvk.sh), well behind NVIDIA's own driver on recent GeForce cards (no DLSS frame generation, weaker ray tracing); no game mode; Standard's whole desktop stays behind a full-screen game. (The newest-kernel track and Wayland, for HDR and variable refresh, are docs/plan-2.0.md's.)

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 19. Gaming on stronger computers (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: NVIDIA's own driver, by choice: Settings › Display › Graphics driver: "Open (NVK)" (the default) or "NVIDIA's driver", for GeForce 16 and newer (the open kernel modules NVIDIA publishes), downloaded and signed for Secure Boot as a package from the Library with Rudolf's key, built in CI for the release's own kernel; switched back by itself (and said) when it fails to load, the recovery system always on the open driver. **Done (2026-11-21, branch nvidia-driver; nvidia-check.yml). NVIDIA's driver is a signed system extension, not a Library app:** 1.6.0's rule (iso/sys/rpk.c) is that a package signed only by the Library's key may hold files for the desktop, never programs, and that only the release key may sign a system extension (files for the system: kernel modules, libraries, firmware), so that a stolen Library key cannot change the operating system. NVIDIA's driver is all of those, so it is the extension nvidia-driver (iso/ext/nvidia-driver: recipe.json, build.sh, nvidia.txt), built and signed by the existing System extensions workflow (extensions.yml, the release key, as 1.6.0's extensions are; extended here, never run by a session), installed from Settings › Update and recovery › System extensions (an administrator's password), laid over the base read-only at each start, and

docs.t: left out when it is not for that base and kernel. Signing it with the Library's key instead would have weakened that check, so it is not. - The licence. The pinned driver, 595.112.07 (its .run's SHA-256 in nvidia.txt), has NVIDIA's newer licence; its section 1 says "you may ... d. Distribute the SOFTWARE provided for use with operating system kernels distributed under the terms of an OSI-approved open source license as listed by the Open Source Initiative at http://opensource.org, provided that (i) the binary files thereof are not modified in any way (except for uncompressing of compressed files) and (ii) this Agreement is provided to each SOFTWARE recipient." Linux is GPL-2.0, so Rudolf OS may pass the files on: every NVIDIA file is copied byte for byte (nothing stripped), and the licence goes with them (licenses/NVIDIA-LICENSE in the extension; Settings › Display › Graphics driver shows it). Its 2.8, GeForce and Titan software for GeForce and Titan cards only, is one more reason only those are offered. (Older drivers said the same as 2.1.2, the "Linux/FreeBSD Exception".) build.sh checks both wordings in the .run's own LICENSE and stops if neither is there. - The kernel modules are NVIDIA's open

docs.t: kernel modules (MIT/GPL-2.0, kernel-open/ in the same .run; source: github.com/NVIDIA/open-gpu-kernel-modules at the same tag), built for the release's own kernel: its version from the release, Rudolf OS's configuration (iso/kconfig.sh with the Secure Boot certificate), the kernel built for its Module.symvers, and their vermagic compared with the release's own nouveau.ko (the build stops if they differ). Secure Boot: lockdown and MODULE_SIG_FORCE are unchanged. The modules are signed (the kernel's own scripts/sign-file, SHA-256) with the Rudolf OS Secure Boot key, whose certificate every Rudolf OS kernel has built in as trusted (SYSTEM_TRUSTED_KEYS): the same built-in keyring the kernel's own modules are checked against (those are signed with a key made for each kernel build and thrown away, which cannot sign anything later). docs.t: Why two layers: everything seccomp, Landlock and the capabilities do is inherited by every program the process starts, and rudolfd still starts many (shell commands, the accounts' apps, Chromium's windows, the Debian container, Wine). A filter of only rudolfd's own calls on all of rudolfd would confine every app it starts. So: 1. All of rudolfd, from its start (before it starts anything): a deny list of what nothing it starts needs (kexec, BPF, performance counters, file handles by number, I/O ports, process accounting, quotas, writing another process's memory, uselib, nfsservctl; the same in the 32-bit table for Wine's programs; x32 refused), and the capabilities no Rudolf OS program uses dropped from the bounding set (audit, MAC, process accounting, BPF, performance counters, checkpoint/restore). Modules, swap, mounts, the clock, ptrace, keyctl stay: the camera's driver, zram, the binds and the Debian container, time sync, debuggers in Debian need them. 2. Each request that starts nothing: each connection is its own process, so once its path is read (before its body or JSON), a request that runs no program, mounts nothing and signals no other process is narrowly confined for the rest of its life: seccomp allowing only rudolfd's own calls (143:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.1: what was moved out of 1.6.0 › Parts › 26. Blitzen hardened against giving away secrets (added on 2026-11-21)
docs.t: The detector (iso/sys/rudolf-secrets.h, one source included by rudolfd, rudolf-know, rudolf-dev, rudolf-portal and the github_pat_ and gh?_, GitLab, Slack, AWS with its secret, JWTs, Authorization: Bearer/token/Basic, Stripe, Google, sk-style, npm, PyPI, Hugging Face, high-entropy values after token=/secret=/api_key=/key=, and a random-looking piece of one on its own), recovery keys (BitLocker's), passwords in their context (password=, psk=, user:pass@), two-step codes in their context and otpauth:// secrets, e-mail addresses (only for what is sent), and this computer's own secrets by token, the saved Wi-Fi passwords and the account keyring's entries (rudolf-portal --keyring-fingerprints, as the account's user: two keyed fingerprints of each value and of its parts, never the value; kept only in the request's process and never given to the model). The same rules run again on the text with its spacing taken out (spelled out, one piece a line, zero-width spaces), on what base64 and hex in it decode to, and a secret given in two or three parts is still found part by part. Not hidden: public keys (ssh-ed25519 lines, BEGIN PUBLIC KEY, age1 recipients, WireGuard's PublicKey, a pub/public context), Rudolf OS's release and Library public keys, hashes shown as hashes, numbers in hex, names in code, paths and addresses, ordinary text.

JavaScript Blitzen writes reached the whole system (serious; confirmed). blzRunJS ran it in a Web Worker made from a blob URL, in the desktop's own origin: WorkerGlobalScope.prototype.fetch (left there when self.fetch was hidden) read "/", the desktop page with rudolfd's token in it (test: "OK <!DOCTYPE html>…token…"); a worker it started had nothing hidden; the desktop's IndexedDB and Cache storage were open to it. With "Check code by running it" on, check() ran model-written code with no click. Fixed: the code runs in a frame with no origin (sandbox="allow-scripts", never allow-same-origin) whose policy is default-src 'none'; script-src 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'; worker-src blob:; form-action 'none'; base-uri 'none', and inside it in a worker: no page, no window to post to or navigate, no storage of the desktop's, no request to anywhere (the policy goes with any worker it starts). The frame sends back one message, its output; the desktop takes it only from that frame, with that run's number. Output and the 10-second limit as before. docs.t: 5. Developer mode's test-computer commands. Every command Blitzen proposes is shown whole in the desktop's own dialog (long ones scroll, nothing cut; the number of lines said), with what is risky in plain words (deleting or overwriting files, the firewall or the network, installing or removing software, downloading and running something, Secure Boot or the boot entries, sending data off the computer, restarting, stopping programs, as root, files with keys); Refuse has the focus; no "allow all", nothing remembered. One command waits at a time (the page, and rudolfd: 429 while the last one is waited for, free once its result is read or 2 minutes after nobody asked). A command carrying a password, token or key is refused, in the page and in rudolfd (never given to rudolf-dev). A workflow to start: its file shown whole, publishing and the repository's secrets said; a pull request: the whole change, a big removal said, a secret in what it adds refused. docs.t: **The time before the kernel, on real computers (2026-11-20, the owner: "add a firmware/kernel/system breakdown ... if it will help to optimize the start-up time").** The steps above start at the kernel's clock; QEMU's "before the kernel" came from the test's own counter. Now rudolfd (rudolfd-boottime.inc), at its start, as root, adds one line to the steps: the time from power-on to the kernel's clock, from the processor's time-stamp counter (a constant, non-stop TSC, its rate from the kernel's log), split into the firmware's part and the boot loader's from ACPI's FPDT (the kernel's ACPI_FPDT, now on), with a handover's first stage (rudolf.t0) taken off. Last starts shows it first and ends with the whole from power-on; the health log's "ready" line adds "N s from power-on" (Chromium and Native). Nothing is shown when neither source gives a believable number (0 to 300 s). Host test boottime61_t.sh (14/14); the check workflow boottime-check.yml. What it tells: whether the Vivobook's 27-37 s is mostly firmware (only the firmware's own settings can help: Fast Boot, fewer boot entries), the handover (the "skip the handover" idea below), Xorg and amdgpu, or the desktop.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 25b. Linux apps' progress on their taskbar buttons (from 1.6.1 Part 25, item 5)
docs.t: Chromium (chrome/browser/download/download_status_updater_linux.cc) sends a download's progress only when all three hold: - base::nix::GetDesktopEnvironment says Unity or KDE (XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP's names in order; Rudolf's "Rudolf:GNOME" is GNOME); - libunity (libunity.so.4, .6 or .9) loads; - libunity's inspector sees Unity running, which means the name com.canonical.Unity is owned on the session bus. Electron up to 43 (shell/browser/linux/unity_service.cc) needs libunity and that owner, whatever the desktop. Electron's main branch (shell/browser/linux/launcher_entry.cc, new in 2026, not in 43) sends the signal straight on the bus, with no check. Flathub's manifests of Chromium, Chrome, Brave, Edge, Vivaldi, VS Code and Steam bundle no libunity and have no com.canonical.Unity permission.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 25b. Linux apps' progress on their taskbar buttons (from 1.6.1 Part 25, item 5)
docs.t: So "Unity" in the apps' XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP would make none of them send. Chromium would still find no libunity, and Electron does not read the desktop's name. The change would also alter what other apps take the desktop to be (Chromium's and Qt's Unity paths). Owning com.canonical.Unity would be needed as well, and never from the portal's own connection: a Flatpak app allowed to talk to that name would then reach the portal's backend. So the session's environment is not changed and nothing owns the name. What helps the apps that send the signal themselves (Electron's next versions, others that use the Unity LauncherEntry directly) is Rudolf's own Flatpak override: /usr/lib/rudolf/appprogress ID adds `flatpak override --system --talk-name=com.canonical.Unity ID` and nothing else.

Everything else is a separate X window that rudolf-display, the Chromium desktop's minimal window manager, fits above the taskbar with no frame of Rudolf's (1.6.1 Part 15, from before the rename: "Standard frames no Linux app's window"). With no window manager it knows, Chromium draws its own frame (the shell's colour, "Rudolf OS", ⋮ – ▢ ✕), and Electron and GTK apps draw theirs. The way (as Native, without changing what Chromium's page windows look like):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 30. Two-player Library games on a home network: the LAN game relay (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: Ember Reach's duels (rudolfos-library, Ember Reach 0.5.2) on a LAN as well as online; the owner: "Go with WebSocket and LAN as the selectable options for networking for the player". A game page can't accept connections, so while a player hosts, Rudolf OS runs a small relay on that computer, and the other computer finds it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 30. Two-player Library games on a home network: the LAN game relay (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: The relay: rudolf-duel serve (iso/sys/rudolf-duel.c) speaks the Library relay's protocol (rudolfos-library docs/duel-protocol.md, tools/duel-relay/protocol.mjs), with one room, as relay.mjs --lan CODE has it. - The room has the code rudolfd chose, for that game and version. Another version is refused with a message. - The games' messages are passed to the other as sent, never with an address. - **Co-op wings (added on 2026-11-23, the Library's protocol 2 for Ember Reach's co-op, rudolfos-library docs/plan-ember-reach-pilots.md P5):** a host may make a room of two to four; each guest is given a seat (1-3) and the host is told. The host's messages go to every guest, or to one seat; a guest's go to the host, marked with its seat. A guest leaving frees the seat and the wing goes on; the host leaving ends it. Duels (protocol 1) are unchanged. Up to 6 connections (four players, and room to turn away more cleanly). duel162_t.sh 15b and 15c. - Limits (protocol.mjs's): 8 KB a message, 90 a second, 10 s to say hello, 60 s silent once paired; 4 connections. Text that isn't UTF-8 is refused.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 30. Two-player Library games on a home network: the LAN game relay (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: Who and where: - It runs as the signed-in account's own Linux user (the desktop's with nobody signed in), never root (it refuses to), with no new privileges and no extra groups. - It takes connections only from loopback and private addresses. - The firewall's new duel chain lets its port (47731) in from private addresses, never on a cellular interface. It is opened just before the relay starts and closed by its watcher the moment the relay ends.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 30. Two-player Library games on a home network: the LAN game relay (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: When: - Started only when the player hosts (the game kit's lanHost → desktop/duel62.js → rudolfd's duel/host). - Stops by itself when its duel ends (the hosting game leaves, or either player once paired), when no game hosts within a minute, or when nobody joins in 10 minutes. The game's lanStop (duel/stop) also stops it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 30. Two-player Library games on a home network: the LAN game relay (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: Found by multicast DNS: - Announced as NAME._emberduel._tcp.local (the Library's protocol names it), with TXT game=, ver= and code=, on the interfaces that are up (not cellular). It answers only questions for itself, and says goodbye when it ends. - duel/find runs rudolf-duel find as the account's user and lists that game's duels on the network. - Port 5353 is shared with Find printers. The parsing is bounded and fuzzed.

docs.t: The owner's checklist (two computers on the home network, both on a 1.6.2 beta with this, Ember Reach 0.5.2): 1. A: Ember Reach › Duels › LAN › Host on this network. A room code shows. 2. Finish, then Rematch on both. Close B's game window mid-match: A says "The duel was cut short". 5. With A on a phone's hotspot or a cellular modem only: Host on this network says it isn't on a home network.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 31. zstd for the system's images, measured (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: The owner, 2026-11-22: "Add zstd compression to the plan" (after asking what uncompressing the system would do: more disk and slower starts from slow drives and USB sticks, for a small gain on the first read; zstd keeps most of that gain). Today: the four images (base 297 MB, chromium 131 MB, modules 97 MB, desktop 7 MB in release 2026112219) are made by iso/systools/mklayers.sh with -comp xz -Xbcj x86 -b 1M (iso/systools/testkernel.sh the same for modules.sfs). xz makes the smallest images but is the slowest of squashfs's compressions to read back; each block is unpacked on its first read and then kept in memory. The kernel reads xz and zlib only (iso/kconfig.sh line 50: no SQUASHFS_ZSTD yet). Kept only if measured: as Part 12, a change is kept only if it helps on at least one of the Vivobook and the Asus desktop and hurts on neither.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 31. zstd for the system's images, measured (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: 1. The kernel first: SQUASHFS_ZSTD (and ZSTD_DECOMPRESS) built in, on x86-64 and ARM64 (iso/kconfig.sh, iso/kconfig-arm64.sh; WendigOS's kconfig on its branch too); the images unchanged. This goes out in a release before any image changes, so every system that updates already runs a kernel that can read the new images, and an older kernel never meets a zstd image (the updater checks it too: it refuses an image whose compression the running or next kernel cannot read, and says so).

docs.t: 2. Measured in QEMU (KVM, the release's layers made both ways from the same root, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH kept so both are reproducible): for xz, zstd levels 15, 19 and 22, and lz4 for comparison, each with 1M and 256K blocks: each image's size; the time from start to "the desktop was ready" (the health log, 5 starts each, cold caches); Chromium's first start; Oracle's first page; a Library game's first start; CPU time spent in decompression; memory at idle; with the disk as virtio NVMe, as a slow USB stick (QEMU's throttling at about 30 MB/s) and as an eMMC-like disk (about 150 MB/s). Each desktop engine timed on its own (the owner, 2026-11-22: "Will native and lite benefit from zstd over xz as well?"): Native, Chromium and Lite all start from base.sfs, so all three gain there; only Chromium reads chromium.sfs at start-up, while Native and Lite read it at Oracle's first start (Oracle runs on Rudolf's Chromium on every engine), so for Native and Lite the start-up and the first Oracle start are reported apart.

How the updater knows what a kernel reads: the release list says it, signed: make_release.py writes "squashfs xz zstd zlib" from the kernel's own build configuration (--kernel-config: ci_release.sh's and build_iso.sh's .config; a kernel kept from the previous release keeps that release's line, --squashfs), and a row "C NAME COMPRESSION BLOCKSIZE" per layer from its squashfs superblock (the compression's number in the 16 bits at byte 20). A list without the line is from before 1.6.2, whose kernels read xz and zlib only. The kernel that reads a slot's layers is that slot's own (the start-up hands over to it with kexec before mounting them), so rudolf-update checks each release against its own kernel: when checking (the signed rows: the release is not offered), once downloaded (each layer's own superblock, which must also match its row), for the recovery system and for a stick; and the running kernel for the one layer it mounts itself (a stick's base

The first update after the switch downloads the changed images whole (deltas find no block in common between an xz and a zstd image, or between two block sizes), so that was wrong. Now rudolf-update's status says what comes whole ("whole", its bytes, "wholeLayers", "packed": each new layer's signed row C against the compression and block size in this computer's own layer's superblock), and Settings says it on the button on every connection ("Download (about 530 MB)", "Download over mobile data: about 530 MB") and why in the card, once; the download goes straight to the whole file for such a layer (no delta scan first). docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 31. zstd for the system's images, measured (added on 2026-11-22) › The choice
docs.t: What it says. zstd is faster than xz on every disk and every engine, and by a lot: the desktop ready in 8-9 s instead of 16-25 s from NVMe and the eMMC-like disk, 11-15 s instead of 17-24 s from the USB stick; Chromium's and Oracle's first start (what Native and Lite pay when Oracle opens) 1 s instead of 8 s, 6 s instead of 9 s from the USB stick; every file of the four layers read with a tenth of xz's processor time (3.5 s against 36 s). In this kernel squashfs unpacks with one decompressor at a time (SQUASHFS_DECOMP_SINGLE, the default), so xz's slow unpacking is felt in full. The levels hardly differ in reading speed (zstd's speed is nearly independent of its level); they differ in size: 15 makes the largest, 19 and 22 the same with 1 MB blocks (22 is 32 KB smaller in all), 256 KB blocks are about 6 % larger and save 10-15 MiB at idle on Chromium and Native. lz4 reads fastest from NVMe but is 43-45 % larger, and from the USB stick it is slower than zstd (more to read at 30 MB/s). Memory at idle

(Level 19, 1 MB comes out the same within the health log's one-second steps and the same size; 22 is taken as the rule takes it. It takes about 3 minutes longer to make in CI.) Every image packed with zstd level 22 and 1 MB blocks, as item 2's numbers chose (the PR "step 2's numbers": no disk or engine slower than with xz, so switched): one place says it, iso/systools/sqopts.sh, read by mklayers.sh (x86-64 and ARM64; a mksquashfs without zstd is not used), ci_release.sh, testkernel.sh and arm64_kernel.sh. ci_release.sh rebuilds only a layer whose files changed, so a layer kept from the previous (xz) release would have stayed xz: its repack_layers makes every layer not packed as sqopts.sh says again from its own files (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH passed through sudo), the same bytes as one made fresh from the same files, and says so in the release notes. docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 32. Emu's Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast games, played for real (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: The test games (iso/qt/emu/, made fresh by each check, never committed; no Nintendo or Sega code, BIOS or game): - mkn64.py: a Nintendo 64 program, MIPS code assembled by the script. It shows red, green while A is held and blue while Start is held, drawn by the CPU and by the RDP. The first press of A writes "RUDOLF64" to EEPROM. It comes as .z64, .n64 and .v64. There is no IPL3, Nintendo's or libdragon's: Mupen64Plus' HLE boot copies the header's boot area into the RSP's memory and runs it, so the program itself sits there. (It would not start on a real console.) - mkdc.py: a Dreamcast program, SH-4 code assembled by the script, with the same colours (the controller is read through the Maple bus). It comes on a .gdi (three tracks with ISO 9660 written by the script) and a DiscJuggler .cdi (1ST_READ.BIN scrambled, as on a CD). The check makes a .chd from the .gdi with chdman. The IP.BIN is the script's own: its header fields, and at 0x300 a jump to 1ST_READ.BIN. KallistiOS's makeip was not used. Flycast boots it with its HLE BIOS (reios), with no BIOS files.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 32. Emu's Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast games, played for real (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: The check (.github/workflows/emu-native-check.yml, iso/qt/host/emunat162_t.py): - Both apps are installed from Flathub, system-wide. The real rudolfd and rudolf-display (as the window manager) run in private mount and network namespaces, on Xvfb, with a virtual Xbox 360-style gamepad (uinput). - Each game is added with games/import and started with native/run. Each must show red full screen, turn green with A held (gamepad and keyboard) and blue with Start held. N64's EEPROM must land in RMG's own folder. - Each emulator must end three ways with nothing left running: its window closed (Rudolf's close button), its own key (RMG's F12), and Emu's native/stop.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.2: what waits on the owner's own hardware › Parts › 32. Emu's Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast games, played for real (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: Found and fixed (PR "Emu: N64 and Dreamcast games start, have controls and end"; tests emunatrun162_t.sh with a stand-in flatpak, emunatsetup162_t.sh): 1. native/run freed qparam's static buffer. rudolfd ended ("free(): invalid pointer") on every N64 or Dreamcast game started, so no game ever started on 1.6.1. 2. RMG's input plugin connects no controller until its settings have been saved once, and Emu starts it with --nogui, so N64 games had no controls. emu-native-setup (run as the player before the app) gives player 1 a profile, once: Automatic, with RMG's own gamepad fallback and Rudolf's keys. A saved profile is kept. 3. RMG got --quit-after-emulation, so F12 (its Shutdown) closes it; otherwise an empty window stayed. Emu's N64 note said "Esc ends the game; F4 opens its settings": Esc does nothing there and F4 limits the frame rate. It now says F12, the keys, and Ctrl+I for the controller settings. 4. native/stop left the emulator running. su starts the app in a session of its own, so the signals reached su and Flatpak's first bwrap only. flatpak run --die-with-parent now ends the sandbox with su (Sober's too).

docs.t: rudolf-native's WebKit is what the owner's Vivobook runs, so the saving there would be a few MB, far below the 40 MB aim, for about 3.5 MB more in the release and another list to keep up to date. WebKit's JavaScriptCore keeps much less of the script it never runs than Chromium does; what a WebKit web process holds is mostly its own floor and what the page does as it signs in. The real fix is Part 39's native Task Manager (aim 15 to 40 MB). What stays from this step: the measuring tool (iso/qt/shell2/lean162m.js: coverage, and memory read without automation), Task Manager's stand-in answers for the stand-in rudolfd (iso/qt/host/fixtures/tm62.json, native_rd.py's DIR/tm.json), and these readings, for Part 39's comparisons.

docs.t: Step 4, Settings panel by panel (measured, not done): Settings in Chromium is 100-104 MB. A small page keeping every module the coverage saw Settings run (107) gave 99-101 MB, the same. A page per panel would start from about what Task Manager's small page cost (60 MB in Chromium, about 3 % less than the whole page in WebKit), plus the panel's 15 to 41 modules. That would save at most 30-35 MB, below the 40 MB bar. It would also change how Settings moves between panels: each panel would be a page of its own, or the rest of the page would be read at the first panel change, back to the whole page. So it is written up as not worth it. Settings' memory is Part 39's native Settings (moved into 1.6.2 by the owner, 2026-11-23).

Suitable for Rudolf OS: yes. docs/plan-2.0.md's "How a native app is built" needs nothing of 2.0's: C and GTK 3 as rudolf-native (already in the system layer, on X11 as Rudolf OS is), one program per app, librudolf-ui (iso/sys/ui/) for the look and rudolfd's client, files and settings through rudolfd. docs.t: Why the account had a fresh prefix (item 1): nothing in Rudolf OS makes ~/.wine (no wineboot or WINEPREFIX anywhere in the source); Wine makes it itself the first time any Wine program runs as a user whose prefix does not exist. Starport GE's launcher does not (its cd fails before wine runs). So it was the first Wine run as the account. The account's folder was not new: its user is acct1001, the first account user made on this computer, and a uid is never given again (rudolfd-users.inc), so a re-made account would be acct1002 or later; au_migrate only changes ownership inside the account's folder and never makes or moves a prefix; 1.6.2b's installation (promoted ~17:40 CST) and Native as the default (#620, in r2026112223) came after 08:30 that day. 08:30 UTC is Wine Notepad ran through Xwayland in the owner's Debian, as the account: almost certainly that run made the prefix (the owner's checklist below confirms the time). Fingerprint readers (from the owner's question of 2026-11-23)
docs.t: A dedicated fingerprint sensor is needed (in the power button, a corner of the touchpad, a pad beside the keyboard, or a USB reader): a touchscreen or touchpad senses at a few millimetres, far too coarse for a fingerprint's ridges. What it does: a fingerprint unlocks the lock screen and answers administrator prompts; the password always still works. Never the first sign-in after a restart: the account's file key (1.5.6, fscrypt) is unwrapped by the password, and a fingerprint cannot unwrap it without keeping the key where a fingerprint opens it (the TPM, as Windows Hello: a later part, if ever). Never instead of two-step sign-in's second step. Five failed tries: the password.

docs.t: Step 1 (branch fingerprints-1): the system's side. One change to the design above, for the owner to see: **no fprintd.** fprintd is a D-Bus service that checks each caller with polkit; with only rudolfd asking, it would add a system bus name, polkit (which Rudolf OS does not have) and a daemon, and protect nothing more. Instead a root helper, fprint (iso/sys/rudolf-fprint.c, /usr/lib/rudolf/root/fprint, run by rudolf-rootd for rudolfd like the other root helpers), talks to libfprint itself for each request and ends: nothing listens, there is no service to ask (the listeners list says so). Its capabilities: CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH only (to read the account's folder's key identifier), dropped with no_new_privs before the reader is opened; Landlock with the confinement switch on. - The prints are each account's own, in PERSIST/fprint/ACCOUNT (root's 0700), **encrypted by the kernel under the account's file key** (the same fscrypt key as its home folder, as Oracle's encrypted folder is). The password unwraps that key, so the prints can be read only while the account's files are open: after a restart or a sign-out nobody, root included, can read or use them, and a copy of the disk holds them encrypted. After a finger, two-step sign-in's code is still asked (the authenticator's secret opened with the password's key the session holds, as after the password); an account with security keys is not offered a finger (its key's step needs the password). The administrator's prompt offers the signed-in administrator's finger; where rudolfd checks the answer itself ({cred:1}), the finger's one-time answer (fp/verify's "t", 60 s, once) goes in place of the password ("fp:"+t, taken by desk_admin_check and desktop/admin). Small hooks in core25.js (__lockOpened, __elevOpened, __lockPw); the rest in fprint63.js. - **Native (rudolf-native.c, fp_*):** the same line on its lock screen; desktop/unlock {"f":true} waits (20 s, again and again) for the session account's finger; an authenticator app: 401 {"need":"code","ft"} and the code sent with that one-time answer

docs.t: Fresh when the tooltip opens: measured when the mouse has rested on the tab, again every few seconds while it shows, never while no tooltip is shown. How it is known. Chromium does not say which process shows which Controlled Frame, so rudolf-launch (which already measures each page's JavaScript memory for Task Manager while it looks, over Chromium's private pipe) asks the shell's window for a trace of its frames (DevTools' "TracingStartedInBrowser": every frame of the window and its tabs, each with its process), reads each of those processes' Pss and RssAnon (/proc, the same user), and writes them beside the pages it already writes, the address of each frame as a hash, not in the clear. In Oracle's own Chromium (Native, and the encrypted setting on the Chromium desktop; also the Tor windows) its own rudolf-launch does the same for each of its windows into a file of its own, which rudolfd's existing processes reply passes on with the rest (no new request). Lite: WebKit does not say which of its page processes shows which tab, so Lite's tooltip says so and gives what can be known: the page processes of Lite together. Tests: the tooltip's text for each

On the Chromium desktop, Oracle's tabs are real tabs inside the desktop page (Controlled Frames, desktop/tabs26.js), each account in its own partition of the desktop's one shared browser profile (encrypted by this computer's TPM key, 1.6.1 Part 20). With "Keep my websites encrypted with my account" on (1.6.0 Part 22, oraenc60.js; #583), Oracle runs instead in a Chromium of its own whose profile is the account's encrypted folder (/persist/oracle/ID, the home folder's key, locked at sign-out), as a separate window (1.6.2 Part 29 frames it). Turning the setting off brings the tabs back into the page. The way to have both (to be proven first): while the account is signed in, rudolfd mounts the account's encrypted Oracle folder over that account's partition's storage folder inside the desktop's Chromium profile (bind mount, as Documents are mounted over /home/rudolf for Linux apps); at sign-out the partition's tabs are closed, Chromium is made to let go of the partition's files, then the mount is taken away and the folder locked. docs.t: 1. Room, made in Windows first. The person shrinks Windows' partition in Windows' own Disk Management (Shrink Volume), which knows NTFS, BitLocker, the page file and hibernation; Rudolf OS uses only unallocated space and never resizes or writes to a Windows partition. The installer shows the disk's partitions by name, size and kind (EFI system, Microsoft reserved, Windows, recovery, free) and offers only a free area of at least 16 GB. Before that, Rudolf OS's own guide (and Settings' text) says how: back up, note the BitLocker recovery key (aka.ms/myrecoverykey), turn off Windows' Fast Startup, then Disk Management > Shrink Volume.

docs.t: The script: the shell's script in the tab's isolated world (Chromium: the Controlled Frame's content script in a world of its own; Lite: WebKit's user script in the "rudolf" world), which the page's own scripts cannot see or call. It finds sign-in forms (a password field, the name or e-mail field before it) and tells Oracle only the form's origin and that a password was typed; the password itself goes to Oracle only when the person says "Save". "Save your password for example.com?" after a sign-in form is sent (Save, Never for this site, Not now), kept for that exact origin (scheme, host and port: never a look-alike host, another subdomain or a cross-origin frame).

docs.t: Filled only after a click: the key in the password field, or the account chosen from it; never by itself, never in a frame of another origin, never on an http: page (local addresses included), never in a hidden field. docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-13: the whole of Rudolf OS as built so far converted to the native desktop. The shell first (docs/plan-1.6.0.md Part 12: everything the web desktop's shell has, Native the default), then every app rewritten as a native program, one at a time, in this plan. 2.0 is released when the apps in waves 1 to 3 are native. Its name: WendigOS (the owner, 2026-11-22: "Rudolf Kryptonite is going to receive a name-change. WendigOS will be the new name, standing for Wayland-ENhanced Driver-Integrated Gaming Operating System"): Rudolf OS 2.0, code-named WendigOS. The kryptonite branch, its workflows and the logo folder keep their names; a new logo comes in a step of its own. Before: (the owner, 2026-11-20: "Rudolf's 2.0 version with the 7.3 kernel and Wayland will be called Rudolf Kryptonite"): 2.0 on the newest kernel (7.3 and later) with Wayland. 1.6.x on the 6.18 LTS with X11 keeps the name Rudolf OS. 2.0 also brings the phone's own build, on the hardware 1.6.1 proves ("The phone build", below).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Two editions, one repository (the owner, 2026-11-22): "The 6.18 kernel version with X11 is going to continue being developed as the main version of the operating system", and "Rudolf Kryptonite is going to be a version of Rudolf specifically built and optimized for gaming and mobile use. Rudolf as it currently is in 1.6.x is going to be the regular home office version." So WendigOS is an edition beside Rudolf OS, not its replacement: Rudolf OS (1.6.x and on): the home and office edition, and the main one. The 6.18 longterm kernel and X11, built for steadiness on everyday and older computers. It keeps the stable update channel, and the recovery system.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: WendigOS: the gaming and mobile edition. The newest stable kernel (7.3.x, then 7.4 and on: newer graphics drivers, handheld and controller drivers, HDR and variable refresh) with Wayland. It is tuned for games (game mode, the GPU drivers, Steam, Wine, emulators) and for phones and handhelds (the phone build, touch, battery). It has its own update channel ("next", below, becoming WendigOS's channel), so neither edition ever receives the other's updates.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: One repository, built from main. Most of the code is shared (the desktop, Oracle, Blitzen, File Explorer, rudolfd, the security work), and WendigOS's differences are additions: the kernel track, the Wayland session, and gaming and mobile tuning. They go into main behind build switches, and the release workflow builds each edition from the same tree. A fix made once reaches both, and the keys and their secrets stay in one place.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: The kryptonite branch only for work that cannot share main yet (today: the 7.3 kernel, while its kexec-handover crash at 1.5 GB in QEMU is understood). Each piece moves into main behind its switch as soon as it is sound, so the branch never drifts far from main. A separate repository only if WendigOS ever stops sharing Rudolf's code. Work on Rudolf OS's features continues on main as before. Gaming and mobile work is marked for WendigOS in its plan and PR, with the switch that keeps it out of the home and office edition where it does not belong there.

docs.t: Why (1.5.9's measurements, docs/plan-1.5.9.md 12.3a): with nothing open Native uses 854 MB against Chromium's (formerly Standard's) 1,110 MB, because no web page runs; each app opened today loads a WebKit page with the desktop's code (Settings: 195 MB). A native app of the same kind is typically 15 to 40 MB.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: Shared with Rudolf OS from 1.6.2 (the owner, 2026-11-22: native rewrites "a core fix for 1.6.2 as well as 2.0"; plan-1.6.2.md Part 39): the native apps and librudolf-ui are built from main for both editions, with no build switch, ordered for Rudolf OS by the memory they save (librudolf-ui, Task Manager, then Settings, then the Office apps); WendigOS uses the same apps.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: C and GTK 3, as rudolf-native: the system layer already has GTK 3, cairo, Pango and GStreamer (for WebKitGTK), so most apps need no new library. A library an app would add (a PDF renderer, a source-code view) is named in its wave with its size, and the base layer's budget is checked by the release build as for ModemManager.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: One program per app (/usr/bin/rudolf-APP), started by rudolf-native as any program, framed by its window manager. A small shared library, librudolf-ui (iso/sys/ui/), holds what every app needs and the page already has: the accent colour and its variants (acVariant, acInk: already ported to C in rudolf-native), light and dark, the fonts and sizes of Display Properties, the translations (the page's language files read as they are), dialogs (Open, Save, Confirm in Rudolf's look), the about box, and rudolfd's client (the token, HTTP, JSON: from rudolf-native).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: Files: a native app reads and writes the account's real home folder (opened at sign-in by rudolfd), the same files the web apps see, so a document opened in WordLite's web version and in its native one is one file. Paths are shown as the page shows them (C:\\Users\\NAME\\Documents). Settings and an app's own state go through rudolfd (desktop/settings and a new apps/state?app=NAME), never into the web page's storage directly, so the page (Chromium and Lite, still there) and native apps stay in step while both exist.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: The same look (the owner, 2026-11-14: Rudolf OS on Native appears and works exactly as on Chromium): a native app is drawn to look like its web version, not like a stock GTK app: librudolf-ui carries a GTK CSS theme made from the page's styles (its buttons, fields, menus, scrollbars, tabs, lists, the accent colour, light and dark), and each app's windows are screenshot-compared with the web version as in docs/plan-1.6.0.md Part 12's rule (under 2 % of pixels different, text anti-aliasing aside). An app is not switched over until it passes.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: The same behaviour: each app's native version passes a checklist made from its web version (its menus, its shortcuts, its files, its settings, what its browser tests check), screenshots compared side by side under Xvfb. Until an app is native, its web version opens in a one-app WebKit window as in 1.6.0. When the native version passes, the start menu, the pins, file associations and Open with point to it; its web version stays in the page for Chromium and Lite until 2.0 decides their future (below).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: Small and much used first, so the way of building is proved on easy apps before the large ones. Wave 1: small apps, proving librudolf-ui Clock (alarms, timers, world clock), Calculator, Notepad, Task Manager (from rudolfd's process list, as now), Image Viewer, Screenshot, Characters & Emoji, Font Viewer, Trash.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: Wave 2: the everyday tools File Explorer (its drag and drop with the shell's desktop and windows), Media Player (GStreamer), PDF Viewer (with printing, as 1.5.9's: a PDF renderer is the wave's one new library, poppler-glib, about 5 MB, budget checked), Archive Manager, Command Prompt and Terminal (VTE if it fits the budget, else a terminal of our own on a pty), Code Editor, Event Viewer, Calendar, Contacts, Weather, Voice Recorder, Camera, Help.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: Wave 3: the large apps Settings (every page, Search in Settings with its index, Display Properties' previews drawn natively), WordLite, WordPro, SpreadsheetPro, PresentPro, Paint, App Store and Packages, Developer Console, Blitzen, Phone screen. Settings goes first in this wave: it is opened most, and its page costs the most memory today. Staying web pages (decided per app, not rewritten by default) Oracle Browser: a browser is a web engine; it stays Chromium or WebKit, framed by the native window manager, its tabs and menus already its own.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: The games and creative tools built on the web: Board Games, Card Games, Emu, Flash Player, Quake Engine, GPU Lab, WOS Galaxy Map, BlockLua Builder, and the screen savers: they draw with canvas and WebGL, a native rewrite gains little, and they open in one-app windows. Each is reconsidered after wave 3 with its memory measured.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Each app's pull request
docs.t: One app per pull request (a large app may take several, each one working), based on main, the owner merging: the program, its host test under Xvfb (iso/qt/native/APP_t.sh: opens, its checklist, screenshots), the start menu and associations switched once it passes, a CHANGELOG line, and its memory at idle with a file open measured against its web version (the PR says both). The release build compiles every native app and fails if one is missing from the base layer or over its budget.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › What 2.0 decides when wave 3 is done
docs.t: Whether Chromium and Lite (the web desktop) stay in the system layer as fallbacks, or move to a recovery-only role, or go. Until then they stay, and Native gives up to Chromium as in 1.5.9. Whether the web desktop is kept as the browser build (Rudolf OS in a browser tab) and the phone web app, or retired. Wayland (docs/plan-1.5.9.md 12.2: X11 for now): planned below ("Wayland", added on 2026-11-15); its switch for new installations is decided at its stage W5.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Measurements that close 2.0
docs.t: On the Vivobook, at idle and with the five most used apps open: memory used, start to the desktop, power on battery; against 1.5.9's table. Target: idle under 700 MB used, five apps open under 1 GB.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-15: "Plan the Wayland migration for 2.0", after comparing Wayland with X11 for Rudolf OS. The recommendation then: X11 through 1.6.x (Native finished, several monitors with RandR as docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 1 says, cellular), Wayland in 2.0 with the native apps and the mobile build.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Why: apps of one account can no longer read each other's windows and keystrokes or send each other input (on X11 any client of the display can); tear-free drawing; per-display and fractional scaling; touch, gestures and the on-screen keyboard as the phone and tablet need them (every Linux phone shell is Wayland); several monitors of different sizes. Memory: about the same as X11 (the compositor replaces Xorg; Xwayland only while an X11 app runs), to be measured (W0).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: What stays the same: the owner's rule: Rudolf OS on Wayland appears and works exactly as on X11 (and as Chromium), checked the same way (same_t.sh's screenshots, the behaviour scripts). Accounts, files, rudolfd, updates, recovery and the security model do not change. Native, Chromium and Lite all run on it; X11 stays as a fallback session.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: The compositor: rudolf-native becomes it, built on wlroots (C, as rudolf-native; small; used by Sway, labwc, Phosh's phoc). It takes over what Xorg, rudolf-display and the window manager do today: outputs (DRM/KMS), input (libinput), focus, the windows' frames and stacking, workspaces, full screen. The shell's own surfaces (taskbar, start menu, tray pop-ups, notifications, the lock screen, the screen saver) are layer-shell surfaces of GTK 3 with gtk-layer-shell, drawn as now, so they look the same.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: rudolf-display's jobs move into the compositor: keyboard and pointer, the brightness and volume keys, the idle count (ext-idle-notify), the screen turning off, and the emergency keys (Ctrl+Alt+Backspace held: the safe desktop), which must keep working when the shell hangs: a small watchdog outside the compositor reads them from the kernel's input as rudolf-display does today, and restarts the session. The screen lock: ext-session-lock, so a crashing shell can never leave the desktop unlocked. Several monitors: docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 1's design (a workspace per display) carried over to wlroots' outputs; per-display scaling (125 %, 150 %) added.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: Chromium (the Chromium desktop, Oracle, its Tor windows): Chromium on Wayland (--ozone-platform=wayland); the shell in Chromium (the Isolated Web App, real tabs) checked unchanged. WebKit (Lite and the one-app windows): WebKitGTK on Wayland. X11 apps: Xwayland, started when the first X11 app opens and stopped after the last: Wine programs, Steam and its games, older Linux apps. Each account gets its own Xwayland (its own display and authority), as each account has its own display access on X11 today (1.5.9 15.3).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: Linux apps: Flatpak apps get the account's Wayland socket (and Xwayland's when they ask for X11); Debian's programs the same through rudolf-debian. Each account its own Wayland socket, readable by its own Linux user only. through the compositor (wlr-screencopy, and the ScreenCast portal over PipeWire for apps). rudolf-portal answers ScreenCast and RemoteDesktop as it answers the other portals, asking the person as the desktop asks today; remote access's input goes through the virtual keyboard and pointer protocols (or libei). Global shortcuts for apps: the GlobalShortcuts portal (rudolf-portal). Game mode, full screen, the controllers: unchanged in rudolfd; the compositor's full screen and direct scan-out for games (lower latency on the Vivobook's GPU).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: The on-screen keyboard and tablet mode: input-method and virtual-keyboard protocols, so the keyboard types into every app, Xwayland's included. Packages: wlroots, Xwayland, gtk-layer-shell, xdg-desktop-portal's pieces Rudolf does not answer itself: their sizes printed in the release build.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Tests
docs.t: The host tests that use Xvfb, xdotool and ImageMagick's import get Wayland equivalents: the compositor's headless backend (WLR_BACKENDS=headless) for a screen, wlrctl or the virtual input protocols for input, grim (screencopy) for screenshots. same_t.sh compares X11 and Wayland screens as it compares Native and Chromium. QEMU (the t160 harness): a Wayland session starts, signs in, the account's apps get its Wayland socket and not another account's, Xwayland starts for a Wine program and stops after, the lock holds when the shell is killed. Each part's checks run on both sessions until X11 is retired.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Stages
docs.t: W0, measure and decide (before any code): on the Vivobook, a wlroots compositor with the desktop in it against today's X11: memory at idle, with Oracle, with a Wine program (Xwayland), start to the desktop, battery; Chromium, WebKitGTK, Steam, Wine, Flatpak apps and the calls sites checked on Wayland; written into this plan with a go or no-go for W1. - **W0 (A), done 2026-11-22 on the Vivobook (1.6.1, kernel 6.18.64, Native on X11), with the owner present, over - Method: Weston 14 was run nested in an X11 window (x11 backend, with Xwayland), inside the Debian sandbox, with Cage, Xwayland, Foot, Weston, wayland-utils, Chromium, Epiphany, the GTK 4 demos and the X11 test apps installed there (the owner allowed it; Rudolf itself was not changed). - Every app tried ran on Wayland: - Foot (Wayland-native) - GTK 4 (gtk4-demo) - WebKitGTK (Epiphany, the engine behind Lite and Native's windows) - Chromium with --ozone-platform=wayland - an X11 app (xeyes) and a Windows program (Wine's Notepad), both through Xwayland - The owner looked and found it working fine. The compositor offered wl_compositor, xdg_wm_base, zwp_linux_dmabuf_v1 and wp_viewporter. Only warnings appeared (no accessibility bus; no xdg-decoration in Weston, so the apps drew their

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Stages
docs.t: own title bars). - The X11 baseline: 1,008 MB used of 3,416 MB with nothing open, 10 minutes after start-up. - The system logs over the test (000563): no GPU fault, reset or timeout, no crash and no out-of-memory in the kernel's messages. The only entries were from start-up: the laptop's ACPI table warnings, and Xorg's input-driver fallbacks, as on every start. - Not shown by A: - Flatpak apps (Steam, Discord, Sober, Firefox, GIMP), because Flatpak runs outside Debian and cannot reach a compositor inside it. - Fair memory, start-up and battery numbers: nested, Weston and Xwayland add about 220 MB on top of X11. - The test's apps were closed afterwards. The packages stay in the owner's Debian sandbox and can be removed with apt. - W0 (B), planned: a real Wayland session from a test stick, so nothing is installed on the laptop. - The build: a WendigOS test image built on the kryptonite branch (its kernel 7.3.x; or 6.18 for a like-for-like comparison, built both ways if it costs little). It adds a wlroots kiosk compositor (Cage) and Xwayland in the image, and a boot entry "Wayland test" that starts the Chromium desktop's page with --ozone-platform=wayland

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Stages
docs.t: under Cage instead of Xorg. Native's shell is X11-only until W1, so the comparison is Chromium on Wayland against Chromium on X11, from the same stick. - The measurements, each on X11 and on Wayland: - memory at idle, with Oracle, and with a Wine program - time to the desktop (the health log) - battery drain over 15 minutes idle and 15 minutes of video - Flatpak apps on Wayland: Steam, Discord, Sober, Firefox - a calls site - The rules: the stick never writes to the laptop's disk. The test session falls back to X11 if Cage does not start. Secure Boot with the test keys only. and the go or no-go for W1 are written here.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Stages
docs.t: W1, the compositor: rudolf-native as a wlroots compositor showing Native's shell exactly as on X11, as a test session (Settings › System health › Display: Wayland (test)), falling back to X11 by itself if it does not start, as Native falls back to Chromium today. W2, the system around it: input, the idle count, the lock, the emergency keys' watchdog, several monitors, the W3, the apps: Chromium and WebKit on Wayland, Xwayland per account, Flatpak and Debian, Wine and Steam, game mode, the on-screen keyboard; same_t.sh and the behaviour scripts passing on both sessions.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Stages
docs.t: W4, betas: Wayland the session of new installations in betas (as Native's week of betas in 1.6.0); updated computers keep X11 and get the choice in Settings. W5, the switch: decided by the owner after the betas; X11 kept as the fallback session for at least two releases, then reconsidered. The mobile build is Wayland from its start.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Order with the rest of 2.0
docs.t: W0 can run at any time (it changes nothing). W1 to W3 come after wave 1 (librudolf-ui proved), so the native apps are written once for both sessions, and alongside wave 2. W4 and W5 with wave 3's end, before 2.0's closing measurements.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: The owner, 2026-11-20, after asking which kernel suits a high-end machine with Wayland, and whether mobile development can be done on 1.6's 6.18 LTS with X11 and also on a 7.3 build with Wayland: "Keep the 7.3 kernel development and Wayland as 2.0 items. Add everything else to 1.6.1."

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: Two kernel tracks. 1.6.x stays on the 6.18 longterm kernel (the newest LTS, grep '^6\.18\.' in rudolf-release.yml): everyday and older computers, the recovery system. 2.0's work runs on the newest stable kernel (7.3.x on 2026-11-20, then 7.4 once it has settled): newer graphics drivers (7.2: AMD HDMI 2.1 FRL, Intel Arc; 7.3: NVK video decode, Valve's AMD reset and memory work), new hardware earlier, the 2026 Steam Controller and MSI Claw drivers, and the Wayland compositors' HDR and variable-refresh needs.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: The "next" channel (WendigOS's). A third release channel beside stable and beta (gh-pages next/, its own manifest, signed with the same keys, joined the way beta is joined in Settings › Update and recovery). Built by the same workflow with two switches: the kernel track (LTS or newest stable) and the session started by default (X11 or Wayland). Recovery mode stays the official stable release (the owner's rule), so a computer on "next" always has its way back.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: What "next" carries, in order: first the newest kernel with X11 and the Wayland test session (W1, "Display: Wayland (test)"); then W2 and W3 as they land; Wayland by default there once W3 passes (before W4's betas on beta and stable). The kernel options for it: full preemption (preempt=full), 1000 Hz, sched_ext (a gaming scheduler such as scx_lavd loadable), NTSYNC for Proton, the newest firmware; measured as docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 12 measures. The phone: stage 1 (its hardware, docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 4) is done on 1.6's ARM64 build; the phone's own build and its interface (stage 2, below) are built on "next", Wayland from the start. The newer kernel helps the phones' own support (the PinePhone Pro, the Snapdragon 845 phones).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: NVIDIA's own driver (docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 19), on "next": its module must build against each new kernel; the channel takes a new kernel only once it does (as Bazzite does), and says so in the build's notes. Its logo (the owner, 2026-11-20): Rudolf's logo in carbon-fibre off-black instead of white, the glowing nose green instead of red (made while 2.0 was Rudolf Kryptonite; WendigOS's own logo is a later step): iso/systools/kryptonite/ (kryptonite_logo.py draws it from the logo's own paths). Used wherever WendigOS shows its own logo (its boot splash, About, the "next" channel's page); 1.6.x keeps the white logo.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: The cost: two release builds and two versions to test; the owner's rule for every session (same_t.sh's screenshots and the behaviour scripts) runs on both tracks. Order: the channel and the kernel switch first (nothing else changes for stable and beta); W0 measured on it; then the Wayland stages as above. When 2.0 (WendigOS) is released, "next" becomes stable and 1.6.x keeps the LTS for older computers for at least two releases.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Decided on 2026-11-15 (docs/plan-1.6.1.md, "The phone, split in two"): the phone comes in two stages. Stage 1, in 1.6.1, makes one ARM64 phone's hardware work under today's native desktop (the modem's data, texts and calls, emergency calls checked, the call's sound, sleep with the modem waking it, the battery). Stage 2, here, is the phone people can carry: Rudolf OS's own phone interface, built once for Wayland and the native apps, so it is never written for X11 and the web pages first and then again. The owner's rule holds: the phone's apps look and work as their desktop versions do, laid out for a small touch screen.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Why it waits for 2.0: Wayland handles what a phone needs (touch gestures, rotation, scaling for a small sharp screen, the input method for the on-screen keyboard, drawing only what changes, which saves power), and the native apps fit a phone's memory and battery (a web app today: Settings 195 MB; a native one 15 to 40 MB). The phone build is Wayland from its start (W1 to W3 below) and uses the native apps as each wave makes them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15) › What it has
docs.t: The phone's shell (rudolf-native as the Wayland compositor, W1, in a phone layout chosen at start from the screen's size): the status bar (time, signal and operator, Wi-Fi, battery, the notification icons), the notification shade pulled down with quick settings (1.6.0's tiles), the home screen's three panels (the three workspaces, swiped left and right as on Android: docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 2's groundwork), the app grid, the lock screen with the time, notifications and a call answered from it, the back and home gestures, rotation.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15) › What it has
docs.t: The phone's own apps, native from the start (built with librudolf-ui's touch layouts): Phone (the dialler, calls, call history, voicemail, the in-call screen with the earpiece, speaker, headset and Bluetooth, the keypad, hold and two calls, emergency calls as 1.6.1 checked them), Messages (1.6.0's texts and picture messages, now native), Contacts. They come before wave 2's other apps on the phone. The desktop's native apps on the phone: each wave's app gets a touch layout in librudolf-ui (bigger targets, one column, its menus as a sheet), checked on the phone's screen size as each is checked against its web version: Clock, Calculator, Notepad, Settings, File Explorer, Media Player, Camera, Weather, Calendar, Help first.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15) › What it has
docs.t: The on-screen keyboard as the Wayland input method (zwp_input_method_v2), in every app, Oracle and Linux apps included, with the account's language. The camera and sensors used: the Camera app with libcamera (photos and video, front and back), auto-rotation, the screen off at the ear during a call (proximity), auto-brightness, GPS for maps and weather, vibration for calls and notifications. Battery: suspend whenever the screen is off and nothing holds it, the modem waking it for calls and texts, apps in the background held back (as Android's Doze), measured against the same phone on Android (docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 6), with targets set from 1.6.1's measurements.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15) › What it has
docs.t: Android apps through Waydroid, integrated: their windows, notifications and the keyboard in Rudolf's own; the list of apps that work and that refuse kept in the docs. Oracle on the phone (WebKit or Chromium on Wayland, chosen by W0's measurements), with the phone's layout.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15) › Order with the rest of 2.0
docs.t: 1. 1.6.1's stage 1 done (the phone's hardware proven, its standby measured). 2. W1 to W3 (the compositor, the system around it, the apps on Wayland) on the desktop, with the phone layout's shell started alongside W1 on the phone itself. 3. Wave 1's native apps, then the phone's Phone, Messages and Contacts, then wave 2 with touch layouts. 4. The first phone beta: the shell, the phone's apps and wave 1 and 2's apps with touch layouts, Waydroid, the camera. 5. Whether the phone build is released with desktop 2.0 or after it: the owner's decision after its betas.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15) › Tests
docs.t: QEMU (aarch64) with a phone-sized screen, a touch screen and the stand-in modem (1.6.0's): the shell's gestures, the panels, the lock screen, a call and a text through the stand-in, rotation (a fake accelerometer). Each app's touch layout screenshot-compared with its desktop version for the same content (the rule's spirit: the same look, laid out for the screen). On the phone (the owner): a day's use measured (standby, screen-on, calls), calls and an emergency-call check on the carrier, the camera, the sensors, written in docs/testing.md.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Moved from 1.6.2: the mobile and gaming parts (added on 2026-11-22) › 4. The first phone, stage 1: the hardware (from 1.6.0 "Not in 1.6.0", and docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.3)

A minimal call screen in today's desktop (answer, end, mute, speaker, keypad), enough to prove calls; the phone's real dialler is stage 2's. The call's sound: the earpiece, the speaker and a headset, with the modem's audio routed (ALSA UCM for the phone's sound card), the microphone, no echo.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Moved from 1.6.2: the mobile and gaming parts (added on 2026-11-22) › 4. The first phone, stage 1: the hardware (from 1.6.0 "Not in 1.6.0", and docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.3)
docs.t: Power: sleep with the modem waking the phone for a call or a text (and the alarm clock), the battery's level, charging and the charger's limit, the screen's brightness, the power key. The rest of the hardware, at driver level: the touch screen, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, the cameras detected by libcamera, the sensors (accelerometer, proximity, light) and GPS readable, vibration. Their apps and behaviour (auto-rotation, the screen off at the ear, a Camera app) are stage 2's. Today's desktop on a phone screen: Native on X11, scaled for the screen, the on-screen keyboard (1.6.0's), touch mode: usable for testing, not meant to be a phone's interface.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Moved from 1.6.2: the mobile and gaming parts (added on 2026-11-22) › 4. The first phone, stage 1: the hardware (from 1.6.0 "Not in 1.6.0", and docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.3)
docs.t: On 1.6's kernel and X11 (2026-11-20): stage 1 is built on 1.6.x (the 6.18 LTS, X11, ARM64); the phone's own build and interface move to 2.0's "next" channel (the newest kernel, Wayland). docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Game Mode: WendigOS's own console mode (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: The look: Version 2 (the owner, 2026-11-22: "Version 2 is ideal"), the canvas's "Home, version 2" artboard: the WendigOS brand leaned into (the wordmark set wide in capitals with "OS" in a glowing green, "Wayland-Enhanced · Driver-Integrated · Gaming" beneath it, a carbon-fibre off-black ground, one green accent used throughout, a frost and night key art with aurora bands, no creature drawn) and what current game dashboards do: a full-bleed cinematic hero with the game's title in large capitals, its progress and Resume on A; shoulder-button tabs (LB/RB: Home, Library, Steam, Emu, Media); a shelf of cover-shaped cards with their source on each, the focused one larger, ringed and glowing; glass side cards for the performance profile (and the play time left on battery) and downloads; the controller, Wi-Fi, battery, the time and the account at the top; the controller's buttons along the bottom. The Quick menu and the game's page are to be redone in the same look when Game Mode is built. Type: Space Grotesk and Inter (both SIL Open Font License) unless fonts already in the system will do; the wordmark stays type until WendigOS's logo is made in its own step.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Game Mode: WendigOS's own console mode (added on 2026-11-22)
docs.t: Its colours follow Display Properties (the owner, 2026-11-22: "Have it so that the game-mode's color theme (the green highlights and artwork at the top of the screen) follows the color theme selected in display properties"): the account's Settings › Display › Colours and theme › Accent colour (S.accent: its eight swatches or any colour) sets every highlight (the tab underline, Resume, the progress bar, the focused card's ring and glow, the status dots, the account's ring, the Library's source chips) and tints the key art at the top (the aurora bands and the night sky). Text on a highlight turns dark or light by the accent's luminance; the accent used as text on the dark ground is lightened until it reaches 7:1, so every accent stays readable (slate and the dark blues included). Changing the accent in Display Properties changes Game Mode at once, as it changes the desktop. Steam's and Emu's chips keep their own colours (blue, amber) so the source stays recognisable. WendigOS's default accent is Version 2's green (#4ff0a0); Rudolf OS 1.6.x keeps its own default (blue). The canvas's Version 2 shows it with the accent as a tweak.

docs.t: How it is built, lean: native C and GTK (layer-shell surfaces of the compositor, as the shell's), never the desktop's web page; the compositor itself does the frame limit, scaling and direct scan-out. While a game runs the launcher sleeps and only the Quick menu stays ready. Steam is started only for Steam's games. Rudolf's own small overlay rather than MangoHud if it is smaller. Fonts already in the system where they will do.

docs.t: Its cost, estimated on 2026-11-22 (to be measured, as everything here): disk about 2-8 MB (the program under 1 MB, the compositor's part under 1 MB, fonts about 1 MB if new ones are needed, MangoHud 2-5 MB only if used; per-game artwork kept in the account's folder). Memory about 15-40 MB on the home screen, 5-15 MB during a game (plus 5-10 MB with an overlay). Steam's client, several hundred MB, only while a Steam game runs, as on every system that runs Steam. Against gamescope's Steam session, which keeps Steam's interface running throughout, it saves most of that when no Steam game is open.
